I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Will coarse grain quotas be raised to fifteen bushels per acre in the same manner as wheat quotas or will they continue to be increased at a slower rate? speakeroldname: Righi Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member was good enough to let me have notice of his question. From approximately December 1, quota policy will be more definitely related to equalizing delivery opportunity amongst producers and as between grains. It must be remembered that producers will market some two bushels of wheat for every bushel of oats and barley and this relationship should be more or less preserved throughout the crop year. Up to November 20, marketing of oats and barley amounted to 94 million bushels as compared with 192 million bushels of wheat. Deliveries to date therefore are not seriously out of line with the volume of wheat and coarse grains which will be delivered during the crop year. Actually barley deliveries in per cent of expected marketings during the crop year are ahead of wheat, owing in part to the provision that a producer can market a car lot of barley accepted for malting or other industrial purposes over and above established quotas. Oats deliveries, in relation to prospective marketing, are running behind wheat and barley, and this is one of the factors which will be corrected as the crop year progresses.
It will be the policy to keep deliveries of wheat, oats and barley running in proper relationship to expected marketings of each grain and this factor will be reflected in the
rate at which delivery quotas are increased. This is the important consideration rather than the actual delivery quotas established. In general, however, the board will work towards 15 bushel quotas on oats and barley. There are certain areas in the west where oats and barley are relatively more important. These specialized areas will be given consideration in connection with coarse grain delivery quotas.
In reply to the hon. member's second question, may I say that although sales, export clearances and shipments out of country elevators are proceeding at a rate in excess of last year's accomplishments, it is difficult to forecast at this stage of the season's operations the total quantity of grain it will be possible to receive into storage facilities from producers during the crop year. If, for storage reasons, it is not possible to take delivery of all the grains which producers wish to market, the Canadian wheat board will endeavour to distribute the excess as equitably as possible amongst all producers. The intent is maximum marketings, maximum transportation, and maximum sales.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night when I adjourned the debate I had been dealing with the particular phase of the speech from the throne having to do with the St. Lawrence seaway. Today it is my intention to deal with matters of an entirely different nature. First of all, I am sure that we all wish the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) well in their discussions at the economic conference between the various commonwealth nations now being held in London. I know furthermore that we regret that the Minister of Trade and Commerce could not join the Canadian delegation that is over there at the present time, but at the same time I can think of no better person who could have been left behind to head the government during the absence of the Prime Minister.
We all feel that probably at the root of the trouble so far as commonwealth trade and world trade generally are concerned is the peculiar and unfortunate position of the pound. Certainly everyone would like to see some method devised whereby convertibility of the pound and Canadian and United States dollars could be brought about. The best way of bringing this about of course is to increase our trade with the United Kingdom and other parts of the commonwealth, but we in Canada have come to a place where I doubt very much whether our dairy farmers and our beef and hog producers would be satisfied if they were dependent on the former contracts with the United Kingdom.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on record some figures which I obtained from the Department of Trade and Commerce. I might
The Address-Mr. Fulford say that these figures are as of November 18, 1952. The prices of products of countries other than Canada are those at present in effect and in terms of the Canadian equivalent in cents per pound f.o.b. the country of origin for approximately the same quality.
We will take bacon. The price of bacon in Denmark and in Holland is 30-32 cents per pound. In Canada it is 36 cents per pound. For beef, New Zealand top quality, average 14 cents; medium, average 12-5 cents; and cows, average 9-8 cents per pound. Argentine prices are presently being negotiated but the asking price for all meat in the Argentine is 18-7 cents. The Canadian prices are: good, average 44 cents; commercial, average 42 cents; cows, average 36 cents. Then we go to butter. In Australia the price is 37-8 cents; New Zealand, 37-8 cents; in Denmark which is a little closer to the British market, and that makes up the price differential, 40-7 cents; and the Canadian price is 62 cents. With respect to cheese, Australia and New Zealand both have the same price, 21-2 cents per pound. In Canada the price is 32 cents per pound.
I have one more set of figures I should like to place on the record. These are supplied by the Department of Agriculture and they have to do with eggs. The figures quoted per dozen are the mid-September prices, 1952: Australia, 52-2 cents per dozen; Ireland, 54-2 cents per dozen; and Denmark 46-4 cents per dozen. Grade A large eggs were selling in Montreal at that time for 61 cents per dozen.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it does not take much argument on my part to show that we cannot blast our way into such markets. Quite a famous Conservative leader some twenty years ago-

speechtext:
It does not take much vision to see that it would not be to Canada's advantage at this time to try to blast our way into the agricultural markets of Great Britain with produce from the Canadian farms. One important thing that those opposite are always trying to say is that we are losing our markets and that we should have more markets in the United Kingdom. Well, we should have more markets in the United Kingdom, but it is an axiom of trade that in order to sell you have got to buy. It is a strange paradox that when we do purchase in quantity from the United Kingdom our

The Address-Mr. Fulford friends opposite are the first to raise their voices in protest, and in particular I will mention the textile trade.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When we try to increase our trade there we are told that we should not do it and that we are destroying Canadian industry. I cannot imagine a more inconsistent policy.
Also, our friends opposite are wont to criticize. That is their privilege and, as a matter of fact, it is the duty of all opposition parties to criticize; but I feel that they leave uncriticized those things which should be criticized and they criticize those things which should be uncriticized and there is no wisdom in them.
We hear so much in this house and also in the press of Canada about our surpluses- surpluses which have created nothing short of phenomenal decreases in our public debt. These attacks on the surpluses are attacks on something for which the rest of the world admires and envies us, there is no doubt about that.
If the productive capacity of this country is such that it produces more revenue than can be anticipated when the budget is drawn up, then surely the Minister of Finance cannot be criticized but is to be complimented. Our policies are such that we are making Canada more prosperous, and Canada is more prosperous than could possibly have been originally anticipated. Had our gross national product fallen and had we shown annual deficits as are shown in practically all of the governments of the rest of the world, and had our national debt increased since the war, then our friends opposite would have had plenty to criticize and to criticize rightly. I can imagine the hue and cry that would have been set up. It would have drowned out every other noise in the land.
I would like to read now figures to show just how our national debt has decreased since the war and what the savings to the taxpayers of Canada are. In 1938, before world war II-and I am using the North American figure for billions-our national debt stood at $4,336 million. That increased during world war II to reach its high point in 1945 with a total of $17,479 million. By 1951 it had been reduced to $15,342 million, a reduction of more than $2 billion in six years. At the rate of interest we are now paying, the interest on $2 billion repaid in the last six years would have amounted to $TJ million per week, with which our national budget is no longer burdened. If we have to contemplate deficit spending in times of
[Mr. Fulfcrd.)
emergency most people would feel that we should reduce our outstanding obligations in times of prosperity.
Listening to our friends opposite and the press representatives in the country, one would imagine that we Liberals derive some sort of diabolical pleasure from raising taxes. Well, certainly, no one enjoys paying taxes. I am sure that cabinet ministers do not like taxes or paying them any more than private members of parliament, or party followers, or the public generally-or even that little fellow the Montreal Gazette depicts every day, a little fellow called "You know who". None of us like to pay taxes. I certainly have no reason personally to love the income tax but I am unlike-for those of you who saw the play "You can't take it with you"- Grandpa Vanderhoof, who asked the tax collector: "Why should I pay income taxes; what do I get out of it?" We realize that these taxes have to be paid in order to keep Canada in a sound financial position, and at the same time to meet the foreign obligations that we have contracted; to pay our share in trying to keep the world at peace, and in order to keep Soviet Russia from breaking its bonds, thereby throwing us all into the most terrible holocaust that human imagination could conceive. That is why taxes are high. Certainly, I would be the first to condemn any government that wilfully wasted taxes or wilfully raised them when they were not needed. To say that our taxes are destroying private industry is sheer nonsense.
Our expansion and development since the end of the war is advancing beyond our most exaggerated expectations. Canada is now considered the safest and best investment market in the world. Evidence of this is seen in the flood of United States dollars, Swiss francs and other hard currencies into our markets, making the Canadian dollar the highest in the world.
I should like to read an article which appeared in the Brockville Recorder and Times as early as September 30, 1952. It is entitled "The Economist"-that is the London Economist-"examines Canada's horizons." It reads as follows:
The boom in Canada seems to have slackened temporarily. Taxes admittedly are high. There is some spotty unemployment, and the people of New Brunswick recently indicated in some measure their protest against Liberal fiscal policies. Seen from "inside" Canada the view of the future may be a trifle unclear. What of the view of Canada's future as seen from "outside"?
The London Economist, one of Britain's most respected newspapers looked editorially at Canada's horizons, recently. In part, this is what the Economist saw: "Already occupied with a load of work that less vigorous countries might stretch over a generation, Canada has the faith, and pro-

fesses to have the capacity to proceed with the gigantic St. Lawrence seaway scheme and to disregard Washington's refusal to participate."
"It would certainly be unwise to reach the conclusion that too much is being attempted too quickly. . . . The rise in both industrial and agricultural productivity since the war has been so astonishing that Canada may well be able to provide guns, factories and butter all at the same time."
Perhaps of even more interest to Canadians than this optimistic examination of Canada by the Economist is the principal reason which the London newspaper cites as being responsible for our situation today. The reason: "Canada is not merely favoured with abundant material resources. It has had the good sense-or the good luck-to provide itself with good government. Its economic affairs have been handled with a skill unexampled throughout the world. It has found in the short space of two or three years, a degree of selfconfidence that is the proper mark of a country entering upon the early stages of economic maturity."
Here the Brockville Recorder inserts its own observations.
Here then is some pretty solid food for thought for those Canadians who cry "it's time for a change in Ottawa", but who don't know for sure just what the change would involve. Looking before leaping is sound practice.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to agree with my hon. triend the member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis), when he suggested that our friends opposite change their policies, their tactics and their leadership. Oh, no; I think that these same policies, tactics and leadership have done much for the cause of Liberalism in Canada. I know that the Liberals are satisfied with this government, and I am fairly confident that the majority of the people in Canada feel the same way. We must never allow ourselves to become complacent or self-satisfied. We must ever strive to improve our standard of living on the farm, in the factory, in the office and in the home. I feel that the speech from the throne contains much that points towards this goal.

speechtext:
In discussing'the speech from the throne this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal primarily with questions raised in that speech which are of particular interest to the Pacific coast. Since there are several of these subjects, I do not intend to take any time on preliminaries but rather to get right down to my criticisms and suggestions with regard to these questions which are of such importance to us on the west coast.
The first subject, of course, is that of the commonwealth conference now under way in England. In particular, we are interested in commonwealth trade. We hope, in fact we demand, that from this commonwealth conference there will come an improvement in commonwealth trade. It has always been of great importance to the west coast of Canada, and for many months now we have
The Address-Mr. Green been looking forward to the conference hoping for favourable results. I have here an editorial from the Vancouver Sun, published as long ago as July 14 of this year. It is entitled "Trade Revival Urgent." It opens with these words:
The coming meeting of commonwealth finance ministers in London will be momentous for Canada and this country's relations with its sister realms in the commonwealth.
Something must be done quickly to perk up trade both ways between Canada and Britain and other parts of the sterling area.
British Columbia is deeply concerned. We must regain our British market for lumber, fruit, salmon and other commodities.
The statements in that editorial are quite accurate. I propose to mention three of those commodities. First, I shall mention lumber. A few months ago one of our leading lumbermen said that the United Kingdom market for lumber is "B.C.'s old faithful." That, of course, is true. This year that market will be about 20 per cent lower than it was last year, and the same is expected to be the case for the Australian, New Zealand and South African lumber markets. I am told on good authority that it is likely that the Canadian west coast will export about 500 million feet less of lumber than was the case in the year 1951. In addition to the cuts in these exports, we are meeting increasing competition from the Baltic countries. That situation is becoming serious in each one of the markets to which I have referred.
We believe that the prospect for 1953 is no better. The word has come out that during that year the market for British Columbia lumber in the United Kingdom, for example, will be held down to about one half of the pre-war market. That, of course, is an extremely serious situation and it cannot be blamed in any way on the lumbermen themselves. They have first-class selling arrangements. I do not believe that there are any more efficient exporters in any line in Canada than the lumber exporters on the west coast.
So much for lumber. The situation with regard) to canned salmon is also extremely serious. Last summer our warehouses were full of canned salmon from the 1951 pack. Since then there has been the 1952 pack, and we are completely out of the United Kingdom market. In 1950 and 1951 that market purchased over $6 million worth of canned salmon, but in 1952 it is purchasing nothing at all.
I -have before me the annual report of our largest fishing company, namely British Columbia Packers, Limited. It is dated July 11 of this year, and we find this reference by the president to the prospects for exporting canned salmon:
The combination of a near record pack of canned salmon in the 1951 season and a very much reduced

The Address-Mr. Green marketing area has created a difficult sales problem. There has been further impairment in the dollar exchange position of such important former markets as South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. All these countries still prohibit the import of British Columbia salmon. Recently an even greater blow was received when the British Ministry of Food reluctantly advised that it would be unable to purchase canned salmon from the 1952 pack. This important buyer has constituted the largest single export outlet for canned salmon over the past three years, having taken from the industry 410,000 cases in 1949, 227,000 cases 111 1950 and 290,000 cases in 1951.
Concerning the loss of the United Kingdom market for salmon, resolutions have also been passed by the Vancouver, New Westminster and district trades and labour council, a responsible body in our province. The same position has been taken by the fisheries council of Canada. They are a nation-wide organization with headquarters in Ottawa. In their publication of October 3 I find these words:
We hear about the 40 million pounds of canned pork now on hand-but there is more canned salmon and canned sardines looking for a market right now than there is canned pork . . .
The Canadian fishing industry has always been dependent to a large extent on its export market. What has happened to many of these markets is now an old story-lack of dollars on the part of our old customers. With government assuming steadily increasing responsibility for international trade, the industry has no alternative but to look to government for assistance in the solution of these problems.
Then the report goes on:
It is to be hoped that the Canadian government realizes fully the gravity of the present situation. Something must be done to restore our traditional markets if the fishing industry is to continue to provide a livelihood for the numbers of persons now dependent on it.
I believe that the fishing industry has asked the government for help similar to that given to the pork producer.
Then our other British Columbia product which is in great trouble having regard to commonwealth markets is the apple. We have been shut out of all the commonwealth markets for apples.
Mr. Speaker, I deplore the smugness of the government on this question of commonwealth trade. During the last election in 1949 the present Minister of Trade and Commerce made a speech in Vancouver and he blurted out this statement in the middle of his speech.

I did not hear that remark. Just a few months ago in this very house we had a resolution introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) which suggested as follows:
. . . that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.
That resolution was, of course, voted down by the government majority in this house. Then this fall the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) came to Vancouver and made a speech. He did some blurting as well. In that speech he advised us to produce more and to be more efficient and thus all our problems would be solved. I have here an article written, shortly after that speech, by Roy W. Brown, who without a doubt is the dean of our newspaper editorial writers. It is headed "B.C. Merely First to Suffer"; "Abbott Overlooked Dropping Exports"; and Mr. Brown had this to say:
Hon. Douglas Abbott's clear and excellent speech in Vancouver Monday did not bring much satisfaction to leading businessmen of Vancouver who are exporters of natural products.
Mr. Abbott admitted the problem posed against timber and salmon shipments contained in the exchange premium, but his smug comment did not promise relief.
Instead, he offered some advice, oft-repeated during recent months by learned Easterners to the effect that "this means that efficiency and low net cost of production are vital to your prosperity."
It has come to be the fashion to direct not a little of what one may call high-class kidding to the B.C. manufacturing scene. Actually, what it seems to boil down to is that because our labour costs are higher than in centres on the Atlantic coast, then we must therefore be Inefficient. I challenge this as incorrect and altogether a wrong picture.
Real efficiency has reached a high pitch, especially in most of the top operations in B.C. timber and fishing. What we are really suffering from is a restriction of markets.
In the loss of markets, we are just feeling the pinch about a year or 15 months sooner than central Canada.
That article appeared in the Vancouver Sun which is a supporter of this government; and just about two weeks ago the Sun had

a final comment concerning this particular situation and the attitude of the government to it, which is as follows. I am now reading from the issue of November 15:
To British Columbia producers at the moment the stirring challenge of Mr. Abbott to produce more has a slightly hollow ring because the producers of this province face shrinking markets for their most important primary product, lumber, and for other things beside. To pleas for help in opening new markets or for bolstering the old, weakening markets, the government-if not deaf-is at least seemingly indifferent.
I regret that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not at this commonwealth conference. He should be there. Even though it would have been necessary to withhold the calling of this session until after the new year, our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) should have been at that commonwealth conference.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the criticism contained in the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) with regard to this question is more than justified when he regrets the failure of the government-
-to take any effective steps to regain the commonwealth markets for food and other products upon which the prosperity of our farmers and other basic producers so directly depends.
I repeat, on this question, that this commonwealth conference must find a way to improve commonwealth trade.
On the west coast we hope also that the commonwealth conference will take steps to promote increased co-operation between the freedom-loving nations of the Pacific area. The conference is in a splendid position to give such leadership because, in the first place, seven of the eight commonwealth nations have vital interests in the Pacific. The only one which has not is South Africa. In the second place, the association of these seven commonwealth nations constitutes the best bridge there is between the east and the west.
At the present time there is no broad plan for maintaining peace in the Pacific area as there is in the Atlantic, and indeed in the Mediterranean areas, by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. In the Pacific we have a series of treaties between the United States and other countries. There is one treaty between the United States and Japan; another between the United States and the Philippines; another between the United States, Australia and New Zealand. It is strange, but apparently Canada and the United Kingdom are not welcomed to this treaty between the United States, Australia and New Zealand, known as ANZUS; we are being shouldered out of that treaty, and so is the United King-
Tile Address-Mr. Green dom, although our two countries are the ones which have the largest number of troops fighting in the Pacific, with the exception of the United States.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Pacific should not be considered a United States lake. With the new government of the United States obviously placing greater importance on the Pacific area than did the Truman administration, now is the time for the nations of the commonwealth to try to work out with the United States a general plan for security in the Pacific area.
Reference is made in the speech from the throne also to Vancouver harbour. We are told that there are to be certain improvements and engineering studies. Naturally I approve of that proposal. I would point out, however, that in addition to improvements in the harbour there must also be additional modern docking facilities. With regard to the harbour itself, there are two jobs to be done. I want to make sure that that distinction is kept in mind - by the ministers who are responsible. There is the larger job, which is the widening of the channel of the first and second narrows and the reduction of the current. That particular work will require study. I think it is very wise to have a model set up to work out the best plan. It will take time, and it will be expensive.
But there is a smaller and more urgent job to be done in Vancouver harbour, namely, the deepening of the present channel in the first narrows. I am told, by the people in Vancouver who know, that this does not require study; that there is already a plan; in fact that there has been a plan for over forty years, and that in deepening the first narrows channel there would be very little change made in the current, so that there is no reason why that work should have to wait for a model. Time is pressing on this work because we have now a problem with oil tankers. Some of the tankers are waiting outside the harbour, and coming in at high tide. The channel is deep enough for those present tankers, but even now there is that difficulty, and when the oil pipe line reaches Vancouver, which we hope will be in 1954, it is expected that much larger tankers will be coming into the harbour, and there will be trouble with them, unless the first narrows is deepened to 40 feet.
We are worried now for fear failure to deepen the harbour entrance may result in most of the oil going down to the Washington state coast rather than coming to Vancouver. Therefore I urge upon the Minister of Public Works, and his associates in the government, that they put in a supplementary estimate
250	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Green for the present year, 1952-53, so that a start can be made after the new year on the deepening of the first narrows channel.
In addition to being Canada's great seaport on the Pacific, Vancouver is also Canada's great Pacific air terminus. It serves over half the people of the province, because over half the population of British Columbia is in greater Vancouver. There are lines running out across the Pacific, to the south and up the coast, and of course to the east across Canada. In a short time we shall have a line from Vancouver to South America. Our airport is one of the great airports of Canada, and yet the approach is a disgrace. It is across the north arm of the Fraser river by a low level bridge known as Marpole bridge. This bridge opens many times a day. I was held up there myself just two weeks ago tomorrow by a very small tug pulling a scow of sawdust. I cannot imagine such a situation existing on the road to the Dorval or Malton airports. In fact I know that at either of those airports such a condition would have been done away with many years ago. We ask that similar steps be taken in Vancouver now.
Then there has been haggling about the purchase of the airport. The government has offered $900,000. The city is asking $1,287,000. In other words, they are less than $400,000 apart, yet they have reached an impasse and apparently nothing can be done. I suggest there should be further steps to settle it. The purchase price paid by the dominion is to be turned over to be applied on a new Marpole bridge anyway. The provincial government is ready to help with this bridge, and all that is necessary is for the dominion to take a lead in the project. This government should look at the broad picture of Vancouver as Canada's great terminus and outlet on the Pacific.
In the speech from the throne reference is also made to studies of possible improvements to navigation on the Pacific coast. On our coast there has been a great increase in shipping. I need only remind hon. members of the construction going on at Kitimat, of the growth of Prince Rupert and of the developments in Alaska. There is far more shipping on that coast now than there has ever been before. Furthermore, with radar, the ships are expected to run regardless of fog. In many cases in earlier days they would have tied up; now, the ship owners expect the officers to keep the ships in operation, and I may say that we have as fine a group of ships' officers on our coast as can be found anywhere in this country.
During the last few months there have been some serious accidents. About a year


ago the Princess Kathleen and the Prince Rupert collided in a fog. The radar was not in operation at the time. Then this summer the Princess Kathleen, which was the flagship of the Canadian Pacific, was sunk a short distance out of Skagway. There again the radar was not in operation at the time of the accident. Later on in the summer the Prince George very nearly ran aground but was saved by splendid seamanship. In this case the radar had gone out of commission during the run to the north and as there were no facilities at Prince Rupert for repairing it the ship was being operated without radar.
I am told that there is urgent need on the west coast for further aids to navigation. I believe that if there had been a fog signal at the point where the Prince George nearly ran aground that trouble would have been averted.
A decision must be made by the Department of Transport with regard to the use of radar. The court of inquiry which inquired into the collision last year between the Princess Kathleen and the Prince Rupert recommended that the use of radar should be compulsory and that training in its use should also be made compulsory. That was not done although a voluntary scheme was set up for training officers in the use of radar. With these accidents behind us it becomes essential that the Department of Transport make up its mind as to what provisions it will make for the use of radar and also whether or not wireless operators must be carried. In recent years there has been a relaxation of the regulations governing the use of wireless and I believe the government should make provision on both these points at this session.
Then steps should be taken to remove Ripple rock. This has become more or less a joke in the house. When anyone mentions Ripple rock the rest of the house laugh, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) laughs, and that is all there is to it. In the meantime the rock remains. The people on the west coast are becoming increasingly annoyed that the Department of Public Works seem to have neither the energy nor the vision to do something about this rock. I have here an editorial from the Vancouver Sun in which they suggest a commission to deal with Ripple rock. The editorial is rather harsh on the Minister of Public Works, the first paragraph reading as follows:
Federal works minister Fournier's admission of defeat in the removal of Ripple rock is a disgrace to Canadian engineers and contractors.
The last paragraph reads:
The time has come for Mr. Fournier to stand aside. He's thrown up his hands in defeat and dis-

The Address-Mr. Green
grace. Let him set up a commission to handle the job. B.C. members of parliament should demand that he do so.
I would not be that hard on my good friend, the Minister of Public Works, because I realize this will be a most difficult job. But I repeat that some attempt should be made immediately to deal with this menace.
There have also been serious complaints in British Columbia in connection with the Department of Defence Production. One of the senior officers of this department, the director of the small industries division, Mr. F. W. Hore, went out to Vancouver in July and was reported as saying that British Columbia defence orders were then at a maximum and that no increase in defence orders for British Columbia was in sight. I should like to quote from the Vancouver Province of July 22 as follows:
Wo increase in defence orders is in sight for British Columbia, though B.C.'s "share" is admittedly less than the rest of Canada, according to F. W. Hore, director of small industries division. Department of Defence Production, Ottawa.
Mr. Hore, who is here consulting with manufacturers and suppliers, said that British Columbia's $29,000,000 shipbuilding contracts are the only big arms manufacturing B.C. can expect. "Higher labour rates more than anything else" put B.C. at a fatal disadvantage with eastern Canadian plants, and the freight to destination is the second major factor working against the coast, said Mr. Hore.
In other words, we are losing out because we are paying adequate wages and because we happen to be too far away from Ottawa. I believe that in some cases these goods have to be shipped to Ottawa and then distributed from Ottawa to the different centres across the country. That is an unfair situation. We should not be penalized for either of those reasons.
A firm known as Canadian Mobile Company tendered last summer on some forklift trucks. They are the only firm in Canada making this equipment. They do business with the trade in the east in the ordinary way but lost this government contract; it meant that fifty employees were laid off. The union took up the matter; in fact it was through the union that I heard of the trouble. I wrote to the deputy minister of defence production and discovered that this equipment had been purchased from a United States firm.
It is true that the price was about $1,000 less per unit but when one takes into consideration that about $500 would have been paid to the Canadian National for transporting each piece of equipment, that the discount on the United States dollar made a further difference of $300 per unit, and that the government would lose corporation taxes from the company and income tax from the men in addition to having to pay unemployment insurance, it would appear that in the long run the government lost out by placing this contract in the United States. I suggest that the minister look into this matter. The deputy minister replied to me as follows:
On the question of securing defence items from American sources, Mr. Howe has often mentioned in the house the importance of our trade with the United States, particularly in view of the very close co-operation that exists between our two countries on all matters pertaining to defence.
That is not a very satisfactory answer to fifty men who have been thrown out of work because a defence production contract has gone to the United States. Later on in the summer this same company lost out again because a tender actually called for United States equipment.
Further trouble is caused through the notices of tenders not being received sufficiently early to permit firms to tender. For example, tenders were called for the construction of wooden ships and I am informed that firms on the coast received these only one day before the tenders had to be submitted. As a result it was impossible for them to submit tenders. That may not be accurate, but it is the report I have received and I hope that the minister will look into it.
This department has very wide control over industry and can influence business both now and for the future. I believe that great care should be taken by the department to see that firms in the more distant parts of the country receive their fair share of the contracts.
There is also much annoyance on the west coast with respect to television. There is quite a long reference to this subject in the speech from the throne, and apparently it is to be the fate of the people of Vancouver not to be able to have Canadian television until a station is built there by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do not know how long that will be, perhaps a year, two years or even longer. Vancouver is told to wait for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and even then there can be no competition from any Canadian private station. We already have a great many television sets in operation in Vancouver, and the owners of these sets are watching United States privately-sponsored television. Just last week a television record was made of the opening of parliament and we had the four youngest, most handsome and promising ministers in the cabinet, although I understand they needed grease paint even at that, in television.

speechtext:
That is a ridiculous situation. The new government policy on television means that Vancouver people will be able to tune in privately-owned television stations in Washington state but not privately-owned Canadian stations although there are several Canadian firms anxious to build television stations in Vancouver. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is going to have competition for listeners anyway from the United States. Why not let private Canadian stations enter the field? I must tell the minister that there is very bitter criticism of this policy on the west coast by the press of all parties and particularly in the press which supports the Liberal party. This policy should be reconsidered. I do not believe it is good enough for the west coast in the year 1952.
Finally, I should like to deal with the reference in the speech from the throne to the veterans of Canada. I deal with them last not because that is the least important subject in the speech from the throne but because this problem is nearest to my own heart. We find the following reference to veterans:
A bill designed to provide greater educational opportunities for children whose fathers died as the result of war service will be placed before you.
I heartily approve of that plan. It is long overdue. Many of us have been pressing for it for some years and so have the great veterans organizations of Canada. I only hope the measure will be a broad one. There is also a reference to a bill to continue the benefits of the Veterans Benefit Act for another year. Everyone will be in favour of that measure. I regret, however, that there is no reference whatever to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Amendments were made to that legislation at the earlier session this year but there was great dissatisfaction with them on the west coast. Hon. members will recall that the amount of the allowance was increased to $50 for a single veteran and to $90 for a married veteran although the veterans organizations had asked for $60 for a single veteran and $120 for a married veteran. Furthermore the total permissive income of a single veteran for a year was raised to $720 and for a married veteran to $1,200. That meant
	|
that over and above his war veterans allowance a veteran, whether single or married, could only receive by way of a small pension or additional earnings $120 a year or $10 a month. Before this amendment was made the figures had been $125 for a single veteran and $250 for a married man. Even under the Old Age Assistance Act the ceiling is $240 a year over the amount of the assistance. There is obvious discrimination here against veterans who were front-line troops.
Last session the special committee recommended that the government should give further consideration to the recommendations of the veterans organizations and particularly with respect to permissive income. I had hoped that there would be some mention in the speech from the throne of further amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and perhaps it is even yet not too late for the government to introduce such amendments. I cannot urge too strongly the need of making further improvements to this act.
There is a tendency growing up in the country, Mr. Speaker, to treat these veterans as welfare cases. Apparently some departments of the government are trying to get the veteran on the same basis as the recipient of welfare assistance. So far as the newer veterans are concerned, I have been disappointed to find in recent weeks that in Vancouver Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which administers houses rented to veterans, is considered by the authorities to be more hard-boiled than civilian landlords when it comes to evicting tenants. There is no excuse for an official attitude of that kind. There is something wrong with the approach to the problems of these veterans, and it is well illustrated by a pamphlet put out by the Department of Veterans Affairs after the last session entitled, "A message to older veterans, employment and war veterans allowance". In it we find these suggestions to the older veterans under the heading, "A few personal pointers":
Keep your hair neatly trimmed, boots clean, and, so far as your circumstances will permit your clothing neat and clean. Your hands and nails should be tidy. You should not enter the office with a cigarette in your mouth or smoke during the interview unless the interviewer offers you a cigarette. Do not attempt to shake hands unless the employer makes the first gesture. Do not rush into his office; walk forward easily and confidently. Don't sprawl in the chair or sit with feet and legs wide apart. Because a man's name is very important to him, be sure that you have previously inquired-even if it be from a member of the outside staff-what the executive's name is, and then greet him with a courteous "good morning" or "how do you do, Mr. Jones."
That pamphlet is an insult to the fighting men of Canada who are entitled to the war veterans allowance. Nothing could be more

calculated to wound the spirit of these gallant Canadians. I suggest that anything they get from the Canadian government is not a handout but only partial payment for services rendered. There is an obligation of this parliament to these men which I, for one, do not propose to see forgotten.

Mr. Speaker, if I make my first remarks in French, it is because I like to hear the walls of this house echo once in a while to the tongue of Racine and Corneille, and also because, during the provincial election held last summer in Quebec, there were increasing complaints of encroachments. I heard such indignant denunciations of the so-called federal encroachments upon provincial rights that I made a point to say in this house that, in spite of these alleged encroachments-exaggerated, magnified and multiplied at pleasure by those who complain about them-we still speak French in the province of Quebec, we still keep the same religious belief and we go on hoping that we will always speak this beautiful language.
May I now be permitted to congratulate the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, who so brilliantly accomplished their task. In choosing them to move and second the address, the government has honoured not only those two members, but also their respective constituencies and those who have recognized their merits by sending them to the House of Commons.
In this year 1952, my thoughts inevitably and unconsciously go back to the Quebec legislature where I had the honour of sitting for the first time on October 31, 1927, as member for Portneuf county. I have therefore been a member of the provincial legislature or of this deliberating assembly for twenty-five years. The other day I was happy to see my friend, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), celebrate the 28th anniversary of his election to the House of Commons. If my memory serves me right, it was the hon. member for Temiscouata who sent me the first letter of congratulations following my election as representative of Portneuf county in the provincial assembly.
I also have other congratulations to offer, Mr. Speaker, and this time they go to the government. Some of my colleagues may know why I want to do so. It is quite simple. I wish to congratulate the government on not having opposed the admission of Spain to UNESCO. As you know, for several years now I have spoken here, in this house and in the committee on external affairs, in favour of the admission of Spain
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier to the United Nations. I have brought up this subject more than once and attempted to be as objective as possible. I had been sent to Europe by my municipality, on the occasion of the Holy Year. While there I thought it would be a good idea to investigate conditions on the spot and I spent a week in and around Madrid-which is not very long, admittedly-in order to find out whether Spain was as fascist as its opponents make it out to be.
I had been told, by the way, that I should not bring any camera with me since it would be confiscated. Still I took every picture I wanted of interesting landscapes; I even took pictures of public buildings such as the civic building in Madrid and the building which houses Franco's external affairs department, and nobody, no policeman, ever came around to ask me what I was doing. Consequently this propaganda about everything being the same in Spain as behind the iron curtain is absolutely misleading.
In any case, if Spain has not been admitted to the United Nations up to now, if there has been delay in recognizing that this country is probably the most unsurmountable obstacle in the way of communism, it is because well organized, well directed propaganda, amplified even at various meetings of the United Nations, has served to conceal that country's real worth.
Through skilful propaganda, the Franco government was criticized for its attitude towards so-called heroes who it is claimed fought in the French maquis for the liberation of France. I have made serious research on the subject and, with the help of official documents, I found that these so-called heroes were born in the very fertile imagination of the communists who had spread all over the world this false propaganda. Hence, there is no reason whatever why Spain should not have been admitted to the United Nations, to UNESCO or to other international organizations long before today.
In any event, I wish to congratulate the Canadian government for not having objected to the admission of Spain to UNESCO; I hope that the veil will vanish more and more and that the door will open as wide as ever, so that Spain may some day take her rightful place in the United Nations as well as in all organizations which are concerned with the welfare of the world generally.
I listened with great attention the other day-as I always do in any case-to the speech of my friend the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche), who spoke of Mr. Henri Bourassa, the great Canadian orator.
;54

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
I agree with most of his laudatory remarks about that great Canadian. He was one of our best French-Canadian speakers, a fighter who fought almost until his death. In some debates, I would say that he was ferociously energetic. He made mistakes like any other human being, but I believe that history will place Mr. Henri Bourassa among the great men of our country.
He made several prophetic utterances in the House of Commons. I remember that at the time of the constitutional crisis in our parliament around 1926, Mr. Henri Bourassa was among the first to support Mr. Mackenzie King's suggestion that the Canadian people should be asked whether the Canadian constitution was binding or whether it could be disregarded according to some official's will or passing fancy. Needless to say, I do not agree with all the hon. member for Labelle said, especially about the C.B.C.
I know that, up to a certain point, the C.B.C. is a government enterprise. He spoke of monopoly and, once he got steamed up for a great electoral speech, he thoughtlessly used the word "socialism" which is so often uttered by our opponents when they try to link the socialist party with the Liberal party. That is their business, but one must remember that words have a meaning and that they should not be used at random about this and that.
I feel that radio broadcasting is too important a matter to entrust it to anyone at all. Neither private enterprise nor anyone else has the right to say that such and such a program is good or not so good or even bad for the public. I know that some officials of the C.B.C. may have let some things go by that we did not like and that we would not like to hear again. Along with my colleague from Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), who is a member of the radio broadcasting committee, I have protested against the broadcasting of certain talks by Bertrand Russell, Anna Freud, and others, because we believed that the ideas expressed by these speakers should not be fed indiscriminately to the public without being subjected to a certain control. Indeed we did not share their opinion, which were often erroneous. But we must not overlook the fact that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a man-controlled institution, as are the private stations, and as such can make mistakes. I repeat radio broadcasting is too important to leave it to the public at large to decide whether or not a program is acceptable. Therefore, I also feel that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be maintained in order that a certain control may be exercised over radio broadcasting. I understand that certain private stations, the majority of them perhaps,

may not take a favourable view of control exercised by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as pointed out by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) in his remarks. He is right in saying that they are not allowed to operate networks. Moreover, were we to ask them to contribute to the maintenance of a national network from one end of the country to the other, the private stations would oppose these suggestions, precisely because they are commercial undertakings first and foremost. The operation of such a network would not be profitable, far from it. On the other hand the C.B.C., thanks to the state subsidies it receives, can operate two national networks and relay to the farthest corners of this country-and goodness knows we have a large country-programs which are quite acceptable to the people as a whole. Private stations would never dare to do so, for financial reasons.
On the other hand, private stations are allowed to have regional stations. As a matter of fact, when listening to CKAC, I often turn to another station when reception is poor, to get the same broadcast over another station. This advantage is due to the fact that private stations are allowed regional affiliates. But to imply that the C.B.C. operates a state monopoly and that it is tainted with socialism-after all one must know the meaning of words. I understand that, politically speaking, the word "socialism" uttered during an election battle or through the new loudspeakers of the House of Commons, may serve to diminish one's opponent in the eyes of the public. But you will admit that there is a difference between the C.B.C. monopoly and socialism. Furthermore, even if private stations enjoyed such complete freedom as the one advocated by the member, there would still be the danger which existed in the past.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to embark upon a too deep and too wide philosophical explanation, but I still say that the hon. member wants to go too far to the right and that he will eventually sink into economic liberalism. Of course, economic liberalism cannot be compared to the Liberal party doctrine, for everyone knows to what extent the former has been harmful to democracies. It is fortunate that the Liberal party doctrine in Canada is excellent. Its definition differs widely from that of economic liberalism, and I believe it is worth remembering because it is quite applicable to the present Liberal policy-it is the progressive attainment of our civil, social, individual, political, economic, and religious freedoms, all of them based upon a moral law. Such are the ideals of the Canadian Liberal party, ideals which deserve to be encouraged.

If, on the contrary, we afforded to anybody with talent, anybody in a favourable position, anybody with connections, anybody with certain financial advantages, the opportunity of making all the money he could, so that eventually a small group of men would control all the wealth of the world, that would be a return to economic liberalism, and then man would become a mere economic creature, striving to make money and benefit therefrom. Those are not the ideals of the Canadian Liberal party. In fact, I don't have to stress that fact since one has only to recall the social legislation the Canadian parliament has enacted, old age pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances, and many more, to find the Liberal doctrine in Canada is very good.
Moreover, may I say to my hon. friend that those who lean too much to the right-to use a word which illustrates well what I have in mind-are bound to sink into economic liberalism which is very different from what is called "Canadian liberalism"; that those who tried to link "Canadian liberalism" with historical liberalism, condemned by the church, in a word, those who lean too much towards historical liberalism become inevitably engulfed in monopolistic capitalism. And monopolistic capitalism- whether my friend believes it or not- allowed Marx, on the strength of a theory on economic liberalism expounded by an English economist, to bring about class struggle after transposing a synthesis of that theory. Then, when the chosen, as they were called at that time, were to be the ones entitled to make money, because of their intellectual superiority, Marx transposed the theory and instigated class struggle. Today, the proletarian class and not capitalism comes first. He merely transposed a theory.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, monopolistic capitalism has of course given false ideals to all who have been disappointed, who have had a hard time to make a living, to all who have had to work harder and who were in difficult conditions. Contrary to those who believe that a depression gives birth to communism, I say that a depression fosters communism but does not bring it about. Communism is born of something more remote, deeper. It is a muddle of the theories of Hegel: the contradiction in ideas. It comes also from the materialism of Fuerbach and of a Frenchman, Proudhon, who had lent Marx his theory on the class struggle. The errors of historical liberalism have been taken over by Marx and transformed by him; that is where he found his inspiration. He claimed that it was now the turn of the workers, instead of a small fortunate group, to take advantage of conditions. Unfortunately Marx went too
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier far. Instead of the unfortunate class being the only one to gain by it, he created another group, that of the bureaucrats. The group of bureaucrats I speak of is not at all like the one we have in Canada. There is no comparison between the two.
This group of bureaucrats consists of one and a half million people, who control a population of 235 million people; they have all the opportunities and the means to acquire wealth, food, clothes, beautiful cars, and so on.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, my words may seem remote from the matter of the C.B.C. But it would be a shame if we succeeded in getting out of difficulties brought about by abuses only to be faced with new ones.
I would now like to discuss the C.B.C. broadcasts to our most remote regions. I am not always able to share my hon. friend's opinion; to my mind, his speech has been most interesting; but I shall not go as far as to say that we should abolish the C.B.C. monopoly. I doubt whether it would be wise, for I am confident that the C.B.C. controls programs more efficiently than private stations would and sees to it that the Canadian people get first rate broadcasts. Besides, if this monopoly is so detrimental to private stations, how is it that more than 80 of these out of 110 are linked with the C.B.C., and relay its programs? I believe private stations benefit from this situation, financially at least.
The other day, at the opening of a station in Saskatchewan, several speeches were made. One of the directors of the C.B.C., Mr. Adrien Pouliot, and another, spoke. They congratulated all who had worked for years to get French broadcasting in the west. It should be recognized also that the C.B.C. affords to private stations, and particularly French language stations, certain advantages.
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) who expressed the opinion that the speech read by the Governor General should be read one year in French and the next year in English. Let me mention as an example, Mr. Speaker, the prayer which is alternately recited in the two languages, in French one day and in English the next. May I say that we are in a country with two cultures and two official languages, even though our constitution does not entirely recognize them as such. However, everybody admits the existence of two official languages. Furthermore, I would not deny the hon. member for Fort William who is very broad-minded and who undoubtedly recognizes the existence of two cultures in Canada, I would not deny him, I

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier repeat, for a whole year the pleasure of hearing the present speech in French and he would not likewise deny me the pleasure of hearing the same speech in English. Therefore, I believe that the speech from the throne must be read immediately in French and in English instead of being read first in one language and then in the other language a year later. That is my opinion.
I have listened very carefully to the speech delivered the other day by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). The hon. member also believes in a bicultural Canada; he has often enough expressed himself in French in the house.
I offer him my congratulations. However, it seems to me that his words exceeded his thoughts when he criticized the government with regard to an alleged scandal in the purchase of neckties-which we ordinarily call "faux cols" in Canada-as well as the purchase of serving forks and of a great quantity of soldiers' footwear. Reference was also made, in the Quebec legislature, to the speech made by the hon. member for Eglinton. Indeed, a minister cried out: "What about the million neckties?" On certain lips, on those of some members of the Union Nationale, for instance, the word "million" sounds queer. They throw it at you with disconcerting ease, cheerfully, as the hon. member for Beauharnois would say. What about the million neckties? Well, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) dealt with this point the other day, and I believe he said just what ought to have been said. What he told was the truth. Besides, there is no point in gloating over it. I notice the hon. member for Three Riveirs (Mr. Balcer) is smiling. We must believe what the Minister of National Defence said, we must take his word because he is a member of this house and a minister of the crown. Last week end a veteran came up to me and said: "Pierre, what's the matter with our Conservative friends and why do they talk about scandals concerning ties, shoes, and serving forks?" Do they think that because we are soldiers we do not need two, three or four ties every year? Do they think that because we are soldiers we do not need shoes and serving forks? The federal government and the Department of National Defence have to provide for the needs of servicemen, for their clothes and their shoes, as these gentlemen provide for their own needs.
Mr. Speaker, I am a poor man, but I have to buy five or six ties every year. Our soldiers need four or five neckties every year. Furthermore, we are aware that they work hard and are ready at any time to risk their lives to protect our freedom. This veteran
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf).l
told me that they were going too far, that they should worry about more important matters, about savings which would really be of interest to all Canadian taxpayers.
That reminds me of a fact. When I was a member of the legislative assembly I often read the debates of the House of Commons. At that time, the Hon. Ernest Lapointe, who represented Quebec East, was also minister of justice. Mr. Meighen or Mr. Bennett, one of them or perhaps both, I do not recall correctly, was speaking of an alleged scandal. The Hon. Mr. Lapointe told him: "You act in a petty way about important things and take unimportant matters too seriously." As you can see it is always dangerous to discuss certain little scandals which actually are not scandalous at all.
I know that such things are bound to surprise. The other day I read a newspaper clipping which one of my electors had sent me. The item was captioned: "Why should I vote for the Liberals?" It seems that a member of the provincial legislature was going about the province of Quebec repeating after his minister: "Tell us more about neckties." He repeated those words every time he made a speech. Then, one of my constituents queried: "Why vote Liberal?" And I understand that he considered this as an abominable scandal. Now, I sent him part of the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) dealing with this question of ties and serving forks and I hope, knowing that man as I do-he is truly unbiased-that he will return that press report and say: "Now, I know why I should vote Liberal. It is because the Liberal party is serious while the Tories are not." That is all I wanted to say about the small scandal alleged against the Liberal party which has been amplified, inflated and multiplied at pleasure by different speakers, especially those of the Conservative "Union Nationale" in our district.
Moreover, since an agreement was entered into by the province of Ontario and the federal government, those who enjoy harping on the constitution and the question of autonomy now feel uneasy since they have found out that Mr. Frost is not, after all, so disappointed in the fiscal arrangement he has entered into with the federal government. Now, in this connection here is a British United Press dispatch published in the Action Catholique of October 21, 1952. These, by the way, are Mr. Frost's exact words:
He added that in this connection Ontario had sacrificed nothing of its constitutional rights.
This is clear; this is a trustworthy paper, one which is often quoted by our opponents.

I have kept this British United Press dispatch in order to show it to my friends. I tell those who are afraid, those who are fainthearted, that Mr. Frost, in concluding this arrangement with the federal government, has sacrificed none of his province's constitutional rights.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, I carried my investigation a little further. I am not a lawyer and, consequently, I must work harder. I must be careful not to make a legal heresy, but I found in a book dealing with the Canadian constitution that in the Quebec resolutions, before the federal pact became an accomplished fact, and especially in the resolutions of October 10, 1864, in section 29, paragraph 5, the following provision:
That the raising of money by all or any other
modes or systems of taxation belongs to the federal .	. .
And in the London resolutions of December 1866, section 28, paragraph 3, the same facility is granted the federal government. Moreover, I think the other day, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) mentioned the fact that the federal government had the right to levy funds by all modes or systems of taxation. I know that my hon. friends say and repeat unceasingly that provinces have exclusive jurisdiction in the matter of direct taxation. But, Mr. Speaker, I know that when someone speaks about income tax, everybody wants to add his word. I admit that I do not like it more than anyone else. I have to pay it like everybody else. We have to do so at the present time owing to the social security legislation we enacted for the benefit of our people and owing to the enormous national defence program we have undertaken. The people of our country cannot cease to contribute, by way of taxes, to those two programs. I am confident that the Liberal government would hasten to lower income taxes if the war in Korea had come to an end. Our opponents say that our country is badly run, that the Liberal administration should be replaced; we need a change, as they say not infrequently, using a slogan which was used profusely in connection with the election of General Eisenhower in the United States. And yet, the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) discussed that subject the other day. He told them what was the change he advocated; it seems to me they should have caught on. I must add that certain countries, our neighbours in particular, are keeping an eye on us.
I read in a special dispatch to the Star dated June 10, 1952, that the Americans are all flabbergasted at the masterly manner in 68108-17
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier which we manage our political economy, so as to make a success of it. The dispatch is headed:
(Text):
Oh, Canada, how do you do it?
Dollar upset humiliating-N.Y.'
Referring to the fact that the Canadian dollar is now worth more than the United States dollar as a "humiliating upset'' the Daily News of New York today asks if the Truman administration might not learn a useful lesson from this and other facts about the Canadian economy.
We move that Truman and company send a commission to Ottawa to find out more-much more- about how Canada does it. This would involve a feat of pride-pocketing of which, frankly, we don't think the fair dealers are capable. But it would also dig up a barrel of useful tips and information which the people of the United States badly need. What ho, Harry?
(Translation):
So you see for yourself what numerous contradictory assertions our adversaries are guilty of-in spite of themselves, however, for they notice them only long after they have been uttered, after a more or less protracted period of gestation. It seems to me that they should delve into the past and ask themselves why, all things considered, they have not won the support of the people of Quebec which, as a political party, they were entitled to expect.
I have before me an article taken from Le Droit, explaining why the Conservative party has failed to secure the support they had hoped to gain from Quebec. This article was written on May 1, 1952, by Mr. Georges Henri Dagneau who is not an employee of the Liberal government, I am sure.
It is well known, that one of the main reasons-
He is speaking about the blundering of the Conservatives and the little support they are gaining in the province of Quebec.
It is well known, that one of the main reasons for this situation may be found in the lack of know-how, which the federal Conservative party shows by invariably taking an attitude which alienates Quebec. The present session-
That is, the last session.
-supplies three instances:	First of all, when
Massey was nominated to the post of Governor General, the leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Drew, kept silent in a clearly reproving manner, while some of his lieutenants vented vigorous diatribes; soon after the federal government had announced its bill granting aid to universities, the C.C.F. party emphasized its demands in favour of subsidies for primary and secondary education, and the Conservatives took this opportunity to join the latter, after fifteen years of fighting the C.C.F. as well as the Liberals; finally they acted in quite the same way with regard to divorce; the Conservative members supported the C.C.F. motion.
That is, the resolution sponsored by Mr. Knight.

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
There we have a reliable newspaperman, well known in Quebec, giving the reasons why the Conservative party should change Us attitude, or at least its policies, not only with regard to Quebec, but with regard to the whole of Canada. And I say that our friends opposite should not speak one way in Quebec and another way in the other provinces.
I remember one famous election, and my hon. friend knows what I am talking about, because he speaks French now and understands it, but I will speak in English. (Text):
I was in Roberval that afternoon when the chief of the Conservative party spoke. It was a wonderful day, and the theatre was full of partisans. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and other friends of the Conservative party in Quebec were there. As I said, it was a bright Sunday afternoon and speeches were delivered aimed at the election and directed especially to Quebec.

The speeches were delivered in French, and I congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on the manner in which he read his speech.
