After his speech was delivered he sat down on the platform while his friends spoke in French. One speaker indicated that he was strongly opposed to any policy of immigration for Canada and everyone applauded, including the Leader of the Opposition. Another speaker said we should have a national flag without the Union Jack on it and everyone applauded, including the Leader of the Opposition. That cannot be denied. I was there and I have witnesses.
The Leader of the Opposition cannot say that he does not understand French, and he was applauding just like all the others. If my hon. friend had kept quiet I would not have dealt with this. However, he asked for it and he is getting it. I am sure everyone will be pleased to hear that the Leader of the Opposition wants a Canadian flag without the Union Jack and wants no immigration whatsoever into Canada. The Leader of the Opposition applauded when one speaker asked that our soldiers be brought

back from Europe, that they had no business there.
Apparently they have two policies, one for Quebec and one for the rest of Canada. That is not what the Liberal party does. That is why we have stayed so long in power and that is why we will be in power after the next election.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address you for the first time in this distinguished assembly I do so with a deep sense of personal responsibility to the great traditions represented in your person and office and also in the time-honoured customs of this house. I wish to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Coming as I do from the one constituency in the great province of Ontario which has the honour to bear the name of the province itself I find many reasons for pride as well as humbleness when I am told that according to the usages of this house I alone of all the members can be referred to as the member for Ontario. There are many other reasons for the mixed feelings of humility and gratitude, yes, of pride which I feel at this moment.
In the short time I have been here I have learned much of the story of the great democratic institutions exemplified in the distinguished office of Mr. Speaker, in the offices of the responsible ministers of the crown, of the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, of the leaders of the other representative groups, of the Clerk of the House of Commons, of the Sergeant-at-Arms and last but not least of the members of the parliamentary press gallery.
My own presence here, by your permission and at your command, I venture to say is to some Canadians a readily understood symbol of the reality of Canadian democracy of which this house is at one and the same time the chief functionary, symbol and guardian.
I refer first of all to my fellow Canadians in Ontario constituency who know me as a plain man working at an everyday job. They knew me so well that they rejected my first three offers to represent them in their municipal affairs, but I am glad to say they later relented and have given me some measure of their confidence in the city of Oshawa for the last nine years. I refer also to an even larger group of my fellow Canadians whom it is the current fashion to call "new Canadians," for I am one of these, though having the honour and good fortune to be born in Canada.

The Address-Mr. Starr
I do not know at what precise point in time one ceases to be a new Canadian and becomes an old Canadian. Nor does it matter. We have Conservative and Liberal Canadians, French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians, rich and poor Canadians, eastern and western Canadians, C.C.F. and Social Credit Canadians; so whether we are old or new Canadians, we are all Canadians. Only the other day I heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) say in a public address in Toronto that he disliked the term "new Canadian" when applied only to those who have come here from the continent of Europe. He said that it should apply equally to newcomers from the British Isles and even to the many thousands of future citizens whose daily arrival places are the maternity wards of our hospitals from Corner Brook in Newfoundland to Dawson in the Yukon.
I agree with my hon. leader, and if I may speak for those most closely concerned 1 think it can be said that they care not what the first adjective may be as long as the second word is "Canadian", nor what the temporary designation may be as long as they feel, as they most certainly do, that their welcome here is warm and generous and that the opportunity here is what they themselves make it by their own deportment and the degree to which they learn what it really means to be a loyal Canadian.
Nor will it matter much to them or to any of us what they may be called, seriously or in jest, as long as the son of a poor emigrant from the Ukraine can take his place in this house, as I have done, sir, commended to your favour by a group of Canadians old and new, of many creeds and faiths, of different positions and occupations in life, from the city, towns, villages and farms of Ontario riding including the historic old township of Whitby, East Whitby, Pickering, Reach, Uxbridge, Scott and Scugog. I mention these famous old Ontario municipalities because I am humbly aware of the fact, especially after hearing some of the hon. members these last few days, that my own experience in the many problems that confront governments is limited strictly to the local field of municipal self-government.
Yet as I have sat here during this session and listened to the discussions of our national problems I have become more and more convinced that the very real problems of Canada's 4,000 municipalities cannot be solved at the local level or at the provincial level, but are in a truly national sense a very proper subject for your attention, Mr. Speaker, and for the attention of this house. Particularly, as I hope to show, they are a matter for the consideration of the present
government; for it is my opinion, based on experience in the administration of one representative Canadian city, that the main cause contributing to the financial plight of the municipalities of this country today is the policy of higher and higher federal taxation followed for so long with such undisguised zeal by the present government here in Ottawa. I am aware, sir, that it is the current fashion of the hon. members opposite to dismiss any such statement with the very offhand excuse that municipalities are none of their concern because they are what they call the mere "creatures of the provinces." It is, I believe, a lawyers' phrase, and I have no doubt that it is strictly correct in the legal sense. But I am sure that the many thousands of earnest men and women who have been concerned during the last decade with the pressing problems of municipal government regard it as the poorest possible excuse for the present continuing and expanding federal invasion of the sources of municipal income and livelihood.
I refer to the mythical Canadian tax dollar. It is mythical in name only. In practice it is a grim reality blandly ignored, it seems to me, by the federal government, but ever present in the frantic planning and thinking that goes on every hour of the day in a municipal board or council somewhere in Canada. I think the facts speak for themselves. The Canadian tax dollar is a representation of the total amount of all tax collections on the level of the three authorities which, under our Canadian federal system, have responsibilities in the matter of the expenditure of public funds. As of the last fiscal year for which complete figures are available, 1950, it represents the staggering total of $4,292-7 million as against a mere $1,032-2 million in 1939. That is the total of all taxation in Canada, federal, provincial and municipal. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the tax burden has increased in this short period almost four times.
In the very limited field in which I have had experience our first instinct when we discover a situation like that is to look for the villain. We check over the expenditures of each department and ask, "Who caused this? Who is spending all the money?" These can sometimes be embarrassing questions, but at a level of government as close to the people as we are in the municipalities we have no alternative. We must not only ask the question but we must also find the answers.
If we apply this simple test to the astounding fourfold increase in Canadian taxation since 1939, we discover the answer very quickly. We find that the provincial and

The Address-Mr. Starr
municipal governments have been extraordinarily modest in their demands for a share of the Canadian tax dollar, but not so the federal government. The latest study which has been made covers the years 1930 to 1948.
It was undertaken by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities last year. It shows that the dollar value of municipal taxes all across Canada in 1948 was almost the same as in 1930. I -cite that amazing accomplishment as proof positive of the taxconscious, budget-wise, good and careful housekeeping which is the guiding principle of municipal government in Canada today.
I am sure it follows that if all governments had been as tax-careful as the municipalities in these years we would have today an almost ideal tax situation in Canada. But what happened? In 1930 the municipal share of the tax dollar paid by Canadians to all governments was 39-4 per cent but in 1948 it was only 12-7 per cent, and current estimates indicate that it will even be lower in 1952. The share taken by all provincial governments also decreased in this period from 22 per cent to 19-8 per cent. These are what our economists call the lower levels of government, and rightly so. They are not only lower in authority and taxing powers but they are also lower in what they think the taxpaying traffic will bear.
What has happened on the highest level of government, the government of Canada? In the answer to that question we have the whole story of the crushing and unbearable taxation in Canada today. Between 1930 and 1948 the percentage of the Canadian taxpayer's dollar pre-empted by the federal government rose from a mere and reasonable 38-6 per cent in 1930 to 67-5 per cent in 1948, and it is still climbing. As the Leader of the Opposition said in the house a few days ago, the latest estimate of the share of the Canadian tax dollar which is being taken by the federal government is no less than 77 per cent, leaving a mere 12 per cent for provincial governments and only 11 per cent for all the 4,000 municipalities.
I can well imagine hon. members opposite saying that the municipalities can get more if they want to, that all they have to do is raise taxes. That attitude toward the raising of money for government purposes is well known to the people of Canada. It is an attitude which they almost automatically associate with the present federal administration, which has increased the level of the Canadian tax burden more than all other administrations put together since confederation. Fortunately, however, this come and get it viewpoint has not been shared by our so-called lower levels of government, and one does not have to be an economist to
know the reason. It is no mere accident that the level of government that has been the most economical in its operation, and therefore the least demanding on the taxpayers, has been that level which is closest to the people and which accounts to them at all times and most often.
The facts are there for all to see and note. In this period of just over twenty years, while the federal government has been doubling its percentage demands on the taxpayer's dollar, the provincial governments have reduced their demands by about half and the municipal governments by about two-thirds. In other words, local governments are today asking for only one-third the share of the tax dollar which they received in 1930. They have made this remarkable contribution to good housekeeping in spite of steadily increasing demands on their services. That is an important point. I need not detail here the nature and extent of these demands except to say that they include the majority of those facilities and services which determine whether the standard of living of our people is to be high or low. They centre about the school and the home which, next to the church, are the most important and vital institutions in our way of life.
' In the welter of publicity that rolls out from Ottawa every day it is easy to lose sight of the fact that the welfare state is no new creation of the central government but has long existed as an achievement of municipal government. It is the local, not the central or the provincial, government which must provide the hospitals in which young Canadians are born, the day nurseries to relieve working mothers of some of their burdens, and the schools in which our children are fitted for citizenship. It is the local government which provides the community basis of the home, which supplies the water, the electricity, the protection from fire and theft, the roads and streets within the community and the systems of public transportation. It is the local government which still, in spite of some contrary claims, assumes the principal share of responsibility for the welfare of our people in those emergencies of life which come to all sooner or later. I refer, Mr. Speaker, to such things as hospitalization, economic misfortune, and even to the problems which beset so many in the autumn of life requiring the provision of shelter and maintenance.
Our population has increased greatly in the last few years, and this has meant increasing demands upon the municipalities for all their services. Costs of providing these services have more than doubled since 1930. Many

new areas, both residential and industrial, have been opened up. New municipalities have been created.
I cite these facts, sir, because we are so often told about the increased demands upon the federal treasury. I do not wish to minimize those but it is important, I think, that we remember that the proportionate demands upon the municipalities have been just as great and perhaps greater; yet municipal revenue all across Canada is no more than double the 1930 total. In terms of real dollars and measured by the purchasing values in 1930 and 1952 the total municipal income in Canada today is no more than it was 22 years ago. In the last 12 years, on the other hand, the federal tax load on our people has multiplied itself more than four times; [DOT] personal income tax has increased ten times; corporation taxes at the federal level have increased ten times; customs revenue three times; liquor taxes five times; tobacco taxes four times, and so on.
How then, we may ask, have the municipalities managed to achieve this miracle of money management? Not, I hasten to say, Mr. Speaker, by going into debt. To the many glories of the accomplishments of our municipalities must be added, sir, their steady rejection of the principle of taxing unborn generations to pay for the comforts and facilities of the moment. In total dollar volume the combined debts of all 4,000 Canadian municipalities is less today than it was in 1933. When we remember that today's dollars mean much less than the dollars of 1933, the real burden of municipal debt is much lower than at that time.
If our municipalities are in a sound financial condition today, Mr. Speaker, it is not because of any high level of income, nor has it been achieved by borrowing. They have balanced their budgets, sir, by the old-fashioned family virtue of not spending money which their taxpayers cannot afford to pay. It is a principle which I may well recommend to hon. members opposite as a sound basis of public as well as private finance.
However, merely not spending does not solve the problems of municipalities. It is well known to every hon. member that the backlog of necessary and long overdue municipal capital expenditure is the most pressing single need in Canada today if we are to maintain and improve the standard of living to which we would appear to be entitled as
The Address-Mr. Starr a result of the great bounty of Providence and the hard work and energy of our people.
We are told that Canada leads the world in industrial expansion. Canada is booming. Our productive capacity, our national income, and our output of goods are rising to dizzy heights undreamed of even a decade ago. For what reason? For what reason, Mr. Speaker, do we work, save and invest, except to raise our family and individual standard of good living? Why sir, they are the very things that we expect our municipalities to provide-hospitals, schools, community services and comfortable, well protected homes, well supplied with power, water and sewage systems in keeping with a progressive civilization.
What is the situation today? The plain fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that we are lagging behind in all these things. We are not getting the benefits of the boom because our municipal governments are being denied a fair share of the Canadian tax dollar. What good is prosperity expressed only in terms of million and billion dollar industrial plants, if it does not reflect on the home and the standard of living of the residential community?
Not far from the borders of my own constituency of Ontario we have the billion dollar mile on the eastern limits of Toronto. It is a magnificent industrial achievement, the credit for which, incidentally, must be given to wise and farsighted municipal government in the township of Scarborough. Here we see the industrial boom at its biggest and best. Huge new plants by the dozen have been rushed to completion along both sides of what was a farm road a few years ago. Already a billion dollars has been invested in plant and equipment in that fabulous mile, and more is being added every week.
Only a few miles away-15 at the most- there is a thriving village in my constituency. It is no backwoods hamlet. It is an old community settled 150 years ago by United Empire Loyalists and situated on Ontario's main street, the great east to west thoroughfare linking Toronto and Montreal. On a clear day you can see the smoke rising from the factories along the billion dollar mile; and yet, Mr. Speaker, the residents of Pickering village eanot afford a municipal water system, surely one of the earliest

The Address-Mr. Starr evidences of progress in community living in this country. Indeed, sir, when there was severe drought in that area last month, some of the trucks hauling supplies for the billion dollar mile had to be diverted to the town of Whitby to haul water by the tankful for the homes of Pickering.
It may be said, of course, that Pickering could have water if its citizens were willing to pay for it. That is true. But it is also true that they have investigated the matter thoroughly and have reached the conclusion, expressed at the polls last December, that they could not afford to pay the additional taxes which would be required to finance it. Why? Because, sir, they are already so overburdened with federal taxes that they have reached the breaking point. This is the situation in most of our municipalities today. Regardless of what the opinion of the federal government may be, these local governments, which are close to the people, and which must account to them every year, know there is a limit to the bearable taxation load. They hesitate to add to that burden when they see the federal government reaching into the taxpayers' pockets with an increasingly heavy and greedy hand every year.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that a serious and indeed dangerous state of affairs has been reached in this matter. A few months ago the annual meeting of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities was held at Calgary and those present heard the results of "An Analysis and Study of Urban Growth and Municipal Finance"-that is the official title-prepared by Mr. D. C. Corbett, a lecturer in public administration at McGill university. In that report I read the following summary of the present plight of our municipalities:
Everywhere one goes, on the outskirts of growing cities and towns and in the new suburbs, one sees streets unpaved, and sidewalks not laid. Water, sewerage and street lighting, far from preceding the new developments, have not yet caught up with them in many areas. We hear of new districts where residents buy their water by the pail and where the spring thaw mires the roads.
The same is true, of course, of the older municipal areas. On this I think I can quote no better authority than the premier of the province of Ontario. In a recent speech in the Ontario legislature he had this to say:
The municipalities of Ontario face an acute problem in their efforts to restrict or curtail the construction of many projects which are essential to their operation. Facilities such as water supply
[Mr. Starr.1

systems, street car and bus lines, streets, schools and disposal plants which may have been adequate a decade ago are now breaking down under the wear and tear of trying to provide services for their populations which in many instances have increased by 50 per cent.
The municipalities of all our provinces face the same problems. We may call these organizations of local government by different names-counties, parishes, townships, cities, towns or villages-but in the long run they are all part of a level of government which is just as essential to the federal principle as are the provinces or the government of Canada. It will be, indeed, a catastrophe if the time should ever come when they are forced into obscurity or insignificance by the taxation grab of any other level of government. This, to my way of thinking, is the real danger of the centralization of so many of the functions and powers of government here in Ottawa.
On the other hand it will be just as much a calamity if the municipalities are forced, by the sheer necessity of everyday problems, to so increase the taxation load that home owning becomes in Canada a mark either of great wealth or economic folly. I need not remind hon. members that no less than 80 per cent of all municipal taxation is borne by real estate. There are other sources of income but our municipalities, far from reaching out to impose more and more taxes, have deliberately restricted their own sources of income in the public interest. It is true that we have a municipal sales tax in a few cities, and taxes on gas and electric bills in another. We hope these are temporary expedients only, and that in time they will be made unnecessary by wiser taxation policies of the federal government. It is not so long ago, Mr. Speaker, that we had a general levy of municipal income taxes in this country. We shall all hope that their return will never be forced upon our local governments.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I may be asked what the federal government should do, in an immediate and constructive way, to help this critical situation. I do not have to go far afield to find the answer. In the first place there must be a re-balancing of the taxation books between the federal government on the one hand and the provinces and municipalities on the other. In other words the central government must learn-as we have all to learn in our private lives-to get along with less. Taxation must be reduced.

Particularly the federal share of the Canadian tax dollar must be brought within reason to allow the municipalities to levy taxes which are at least close to being within keeping with the increased demands on their resources. After all, this relationship between federal, provincial and municipal governments is a family affair. There is only so much money in the family budget, and if one member of the family takes more than he needs, the others must suffer. We do not say that all should share equally, but it does seem to make sense that each should participate in the family finances, not according to his strength, size or power, but according to his needs as agreed upon in family council.
And that is my second suggestion, Mr. Speaker; the calling of a friendly family council to discuss these matters. Specifically I suggest the reconvening of the economic committee that was set up with such high hopes a few years ago during the federal-provincial discussions of the immediate postwar years. It met, I believe, in December 1945 and in January 1946. Then it faded somehow out of existence. The municipalities of Canada have asked that it be reconvened on a very wide basis of representation, and I urge the government to give this immediate consideration.
There are many things which could be worked out to the mutual satisfaction and advantage of all of us in such a setting. To mention only two, there is the taxation of crown property and crown companies; the exemption of municipal purchases from the federal sales tax to the same extent and for the same good reasons that provincial purchases are now exempt.
These very questions, f am informed, will be brought to the attention of the federal government this week when a delegation from the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities calls upon the government here in Ottawa. That meeting, Mr. Speaker, could be a momentous one for the whole future of this country if the government will look upon the delegation in the spirit in which we would expect the senior members of any family to listen to a plea from its junior members for assistance in a financial matter whose seriousness is no fault of their own and whose solution is beyond their income and allowance. I hope they will not receive, instead, long and learned lectures on the British North
The Address-Mr. Sinnott America Act or the usual unreal excuses that the head of family is too hard-pressed financially to help. Most of us know better.
Above all, sir, the government will render a great service to all the people of Canada if they will admit their share of responsibility for the plight of the municipalities. For it is the weight of federal taxes that embarrasses every one of the 4,000 municipalities of this country. It is a weight so burdensome and unbearable that it threatens their future, and thereby endangers our whole democratic system. For taxes, Mr. Speaker, may not only cripple; they can also destroy.
The wise words of the great Chief Justice Marshall in the supreme court of the United States as long ago as the year 1819 are as valid in this municipal problem as they proved to be in those problems which confronted our neighbours to the south many years ago. None of us, sir, has any doubt about the power of this present administration to tax us, but we do ask that in these things which so closely touch our daily lives they heed John Marshall's warning to all who have great taxing powers:
The power to tax, is the power to destroy.

speechtext:
At this time I wish to offer my sincere thanks to all the members in this house who have been so kind and co-operative during the past seven years. We have had our differences at times during debates, but on the whole you will not find a better group of men with whom to work.
There are a few very important subjects to which I should like to draw the attention of the government. When this newspaperman inter-

I wish at this time to say that no country in the world under any government has a better record of financial improvement and expansion than has our present government. For six consecutive years we have had a balanced budget with

Ours is a government which has brought in important measures of social security, including family allowances, unemployment insurance, floor prices for agricultural and fish products, veterans' benefits, pensions for the blind and old age pensions. In the year 1951 over a billion dollars was spent by the government to provide these services, while at the same time having reduced Canada's national debt to the tune of approximately $2J billion; and if this were not paid, our tax load would be increased a further $62 million per year for interest charges.
Is it the policy of the opposition to have this cancer of civilization which is called interest take away most of our profits? If that is so, it is certainly not the policy of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), his Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) or his government. Mr. Speaker, to make a long story short, our 1951 tax dollar was spent as follows: We spent three cents in payments to the provinces in subsidies and tax rentals. Fourteen and a half cents of our tax dollar were paid back to the people of Canada in social security measures. Five and a half cents of our tax dollar were paid to Canadian veterans of both world wars and Korea. Thirteen and one-third cents were paid in annual charges on our national debt. Six and a quarter cents were paid to reduce the national debt. Thirty-six and one-third cents were applied to Canada's national defence, and I do not suppose anybody complains about that. Twenty-one cents were spent on all activities and services provided by the government; that is, railway transportation, railroads, ships and the rest of it.

I have read carefully the speech delivered by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) and I could not help seeing that the political creed of the party to which he belongs has not varied from time immemorial since he is still ready to uphold at any cost the very excesses of what they call the incomparable advantages of private enterprise.
Whatever the subject of the debate, whether it be the prohibition of resale price maintenance, the act concerning combines and monopolies, or the question of broadcasting and television, the hon. member for Labelle always adheres strictly to the classical and well-known line that the "profit" motive must alone be responsible for anything that is fine and good in our modern society.
Does not the hon. member imply that the government are becoming socialistic because they have to a large extent given effect to the conclusions of the Massey report on the arts, letters and sciences, as did their predecessors when dealing with the Aird report on radio broadcasting.
If my colleague has that word "socialism" at heart, may I add that there is not much to choose between socialism and the abuses of private initiative. Many countries have obtained good results steering a middle course, that is to promote private initiative while trying at the same time to remedy

some of its inescapable abuses. That is what the present government tries to do by giving effect to the recommendations of the Massey report on radio broadcasting and television.
And now, since the hon. member for Labelle neglected to study the question from every angle, it would be a good idea to go back a little and consider the reasons why the C.B.C. entered the field of radio broadcasting and television.
Thirty years ago, the Canadian people were beginning to take an interest in radio broadcasting. Radio broadcasting was becoming a wonderful means of recreation and culture for the entire population, rural and urban, and particularly for those citizens who had to live alone, isolated from their neighbours by the vastness of the country.
Our first programs, as could be expected, were brought in from the United States for the benefit of those who lived near the border. For quite a few years, the government limited its activity to the granting of permits for receiving sets and broadcasting stations. The first license was granted in 1919. In 1929, ten years later, there were in Canada 10 broadcasting stations and 296,926 receiving sets, most of them located in large cities, and our rural population, especially the isolated settlements in the western provinces, had to forgo the benefits of this invention.
The Aird commission, established in 1928 to inquire into the field of broadcasting, praised the efforts of private enterprise but deplored the growing commercialism which characterized the new industry, the all but dominating influence of American music and advertising, the gradual lowering of the quality of the programs which were automatically adapted to the poorest cultural standard of the listening masses.
Besides, a large proportion of the people, those who live in the country far from the large cities, were urging the government to intervene so that they might enjoy as soon as possible the numerous advantages of radio broadcasting.
Consequently, after an investigation conducted among many groups, the government decided to intervene in order to establish in Canada a radio broadcasting system so as to, first, set up a national network; secondly, protect this propaganda medium against an overdose of American influence; thirdly, to encourage our Canadian artists.
Certain aspects of the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation may have been open to criticism. But, out of 170 various organizations whose opinions were
The Address-Mr. Breton sought by the said corporation, such as the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and others, the greatest majority supported the stand taken by the government on radio broadcasting and television.
Profiting from the experience acquired in England, where radio is an absolute state monopoly, with no commercial advertising whatever, and in the United States, where radio is an entirely private concern sponsored by commercial and industrial firms, the Canadian government had decided to steer a middle course and to aid the public while, at the same time, allowing private enterprise to compete with the official network.
Then, at last, came the organization of television in Canada, an undertaking which has aroused, and for that matter is still arousing, greater enthusiasm than all the others.
At present relatively few countries enjoy television broadcasts. Great Britain, France, the United States, Russia, Mexico, Brazil and Cuba were the only countries providing television services in 1951, when the Massey report was completed. There were, at that time, two television stations in Russia, two in England, two in France and 107 in the United States, the latter being distributed amongst 66 American cities.
The only other countries which are at present concerning themselves with television are Italy, Denmark and Switzerland, but, so far, they have not progressed beyond the experimental stage.
England and France have organized television as a state monopoly, without any commercial advertising. The United States alone, followed by Mexico, Cuba and Brazil, rely exclusively on the trial and error method of free enterprise.
It is true that television has developed more rapidly in the United States, under the system of private enterprise. But it was at the price of enormous costs which could be justified by the great profits made by radio, by the large urban population and by the wealth of sponsors. Canada can neither afford such luxury nor fall completely under the control of American television whose publicity extravagances and low quality programs have even been criticized by the Americans themselves.
It may be that a certain number of listeners are contented with baseball, hockey or wrestling. But there are others who would prefer a much wider variety of programs comprising good music, theatre, and educational features.

Mr. Speaker, for the past fifteen years or so, public opinion in this country has constantly been alerted on the question of the sharing of powers between the federal and provincial governments. The federal government has carried out an ever-increasing effort towards centralization. In this connection protests have come from every province in Canada and more particularly from the province of Quebec. Though other governments may be interested in the retention of provincial rights for financial reasons it is only natural that we of Quebec whose language is different, whose soul, culture, traditions and religion are different, should always have taken a very keen interest in the constitutional arrangements under which we are living.
Our representatives, in 1867, consented to join the rest of Canada precisely because, at that time, they were being offered a federative compact, since it was suggested that a confederation be established wherein the various powers would be apportioned between the central government and each of the various provinces in such a way as to ensure, for many years to come, the survival of our language, our traditions, of our French schools, in short of our very racial group.
Confederation is a constitutional pact between the two great races of this country. It is a document which we, from Quebec, have learned to admire, for it has favoured here,


in Canadian territory, the prosperity of two ethnical groups of different cultures; it has enabled them to blend themselves firmly enough to make of the Canadian nation one of the great nations of the world.
Unfortunately, the spirit which at the time inspired the fathers of confederation seems now to have disappeared and, today, the very existence of this federative pact is shaken every day. The federal government is insatiable and wishes to monopolize all powers of taxation and thus relegate the provincial legislatures to the rank of administrative commissions.
The Quebec government has waged a stubborn fight, a daily fight against this exaggerated centralization of the central power and up to the last few months, it was supported by the Ontario government.
Unfortunately, the whole question of federal-provincial relations has taken a still more tragic aspect, especially since the prime minister of the most populous province of Canada has accepted the proposals of the central government. But here again, while he accepted these direct grants in return for the taxation rights surrendered by his province, the premier of Ontario did not hesitate to make it clear that it was regretfully that he consented to sign that agreement and that it was on his part a gesture of a purely temporary nature. He hoped that this question of the distribution of taxes would be the object of a more exhaustive study so that a new plan could be proposed without delay.
The fact remains however that Quebec is the only province which was able to refuse the mess of pottage offered by the central government. And, as a member from the province of Quebec, I can only rejoice that our province is headed by a government which has always sustained the rights of the provinces, while confronted by the centralizing pressure of the federal government.
In my capacity as a Conservative member, I note with pride that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is also imbued with the same respect for our confederation and that, at the very beginning of this session, he did not hesitate to raise this problem in the house and to demand, in his first speech, that a conference be held between the central government and the provinces, so that the latter may at last obtain justice.
It goes without saying that the provinces have not only rights but also duties. However, by taking over their sources of taxation, the federal government has increased its power in an exaggerated manner and has destroyed altogether the balance established between the provinces and the central government, under the British North America Act.

So that it is really the government which is to blame. It has monopolized taxation rights which, since 1867, belonged to the provinces under the pretext that this was essential for the conduct of our national war effort. But the government had more or less promised to relinquish those rights one year after the war.
The war came to an end seven years ago but the federal government has not yet relinquished these sources of taxation. It is determined more or less to starve the provinces as Mr. Filion so aptly put it in his editorial published last Saturday in Le Devoir. I quote:
The power of taxation as understood by Mr. St. Laurent is the power to starve. According to the Prime Minister, Ottawa would be entitled to monopolize every source of taxation assigned to the central power under our constitution and to let the municipalities and the provinces go bankrupt.
During the war, Ottawa got into the habit of taxing as much as it could and it never lost this habit altogether. It has used the moneys thus collected to set up social services which are within the fields of the provinces; it has accumulated from year to year considerable surpluses; last year, the Minister of Finance collected very close to three quarters of a billion over and above his needs.
While Ottawa is rolling in wealth, provinces and municipalities have trouble to make ends meet. Nine Canadian provinces, several of them reluctantly, had to surrender to the federal government because they were unable to meet their obligations in any other way. Municipalities and school boards are all repeating the same desperate cry: their responsibilities are increasing while their sources of revenue remain inadequate.
Every day the federal government tries to obtain more and more from the provinces, asks them to abandon such and such a right in its favour, so much so that it has succeeded in getting all taxes to flow into its own coffers. In 1939, when the federal government was getting 51 per cent of taxation revenues, the provinces and municipalities were getting 49 per cent. Today, after thirteen years of Liberal regime, Ottawa is taking 77 per cent while provincial governments are getting only 12 per cent and municipalities only 11 per cent.
It is impossible for the provincial or the municipal authorities to collect another cent from the taxpayers when they are being clipped by the federal authorities as they are today through increased taxation.
So much so that during a period of prosperity like the one we are experiencing at the present time, the provinces and the municipalities, especially the latter, are unable to face their responsibilities. And they are forced to seek a handout from the federal government which is piling up surpluses.
The federal government is infiltrating every field of government under the pretext that

The Address-Mr. Lesage
In explaining that part of his proposed amendment, the Leader of the Opposition paid special attention to the province of Quebec, which he mentioned twice, and for reasons which are easy to understand. Since he has become the Leader of the Opposition, and as a matter of fact since he first had some hopes of becoming the leader of his party, he has been bidding for the Quebec votes, after taking a tremendous somersault. Having claimed in 1937 that the provinces had assumed powers meant for the federal government, and that we should go back to pne strong government, he now claims, with an eye to the votes of the province of Quebec, that Ottawa should divest itself of still more powers in favour of the provinces, although those powers are given to the federal parliament by our constitution.
In our province, Quebec, we know very well, sir, the traditions of the Conservative party. We know what the Conservatives think; we know that their sudden love for
o.ur people, this extraordinary about-face, comes more from a lust for power that has been denied to them for so long by the people of Canada, than it comes from the heart. From the very beginning their great chief, the founder of their party, whom I respect, Sir John A. Macdonald, said in the parliamentary debates on confederation:
Those who were, like myself, in favour of legislative union, were obliged to modify their views and accept the project of a federal union.
And later:
We have strengthened the general government. We have given the general legislature all the great subjects of legislation . . . we will have in fact all the advantages of a legislative union under one administration.
How much like the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, when he exclaims:
We must start all over again from confederation, if we are to have one country instead of nine.
How history repeats itself, but how inconsistent is the Leader of the Opposition. This is, sir, the short story of the Conservative party for three-quarters of a century. Sir John, whilst renouncing his ideal of a unitary state, declared that confederation was to be a form of centralized federalism, and this has always been the aim and philosophy of the Conservative party. Let us remember 1934 and 1935 under Mr. Bennett. It is for this reason that in opposition to what took place in the United States, and in opposition to what was to happen later in Australia, the residue of powers was given in Canada to the federal government. The powers of the provinces were enumerated in 1867 in a


very restricted list, being essentially those of a local and private nature, in line with the importance which Sir John A. Macdonald intended to give to the provincial authorities.
The federal government, according to Sir John, in 1866, was to have the right to appoint and dismiss the lieutenant governors of the provinces; also the right was to be granted to the federal government to disallow the laws passed by the legislatures within the year following their assent. We sometimes find it surprising that the distribution of powers between the federal and provincial authorities gave rise to so little discussion at the time. The explanation given by Sir John was that the delegates at the conference had realized the necessity of creating a strong and powerful central government. That is the record of the founder of the Conservative party.
Let us examine now what are the reasons alleged by the Leader of the Opposition to accuse the present government of centralization. I quote from his speech in this house on Monday, November 24, as reported at page 32 of Hansard:
The rapidly increasing trend toward centralization of taxing powers has greatly weakened the position of the provincial and municipal governments.

very little of whatever taxation rights they had under the constitution, and in 1867 nearly two-thirds of the budgets of the provinces were met by subsidies paid to them by the federal government. Since then the provinces have gained more and more independence in that field until they have reached the point where if it could have been said that at the time of confederation the provinces were subservient to the federal government as far as taxation is concerned, they have now reached complete autonomy in the field of taxation.
For instance, in 1937 federal subsidies accounted for only 4 [DOT] 5 per cent of the budget of the province of Quebec. Listening to the hon. member for Three Rivers and to the outcries and accusations in relation to the centralization of taxing powers and against the present Liberal administration, one would expect that the trend had been reversed since 1937. On the contrary, in 1951 the total revenues of the province of Quebec were $275-5 million, of which only $3,300,000 was from federal subsidies, or a little over 1 per cent. The province of Quebec was collecting through its own means of taxation 99 per cent of its revenue, whereas in 1867 it was collecting only one-third. Where is their fiscal subservience in that? Does not the difference between 60 per cent and 1 per cent prove that far from having lost its fiscal autonomy the province of Quebec has now complete fiscal independence?
If you will allow me to say so, let us not be fooled by grandiloquent speeches, by outcries of Au voleur! A l'assassin! Non, ecoutons plutot la raison et les faits. Let us look at the facts; let us look at the figures; let us look at the record. Let me ask this question: Are there any provincial taxation rights that have been stolen by the federal government and that should be restored to the provinces?

They are reserved expressly to the federal government by the constitution. That leaves us with three and four, personal and corporate income taxes and succession duties.
Would any member of the opposition, especially the Leader of the Opposition, deny the rights of this parliament in those fields? Let us consult the real authority on the matter, the British North America Act. I should like to read from sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, 1867. Section 91 reads:
. . . the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
3. The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
Section 92 reads:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
2. Direct taxation within the province in order to the raising of a revenue for provincial purposes.
What is the meaning of those paragraphs? They mean precisely what they say, that the federal parliament has the exclusive power to raise money by any mode or system of taxation, whether by direct or indirect taxes, and that the provinces may impose direct taxes for provincial purposes only. In Silver Brothers and the Attorney General for Quebec v. the Attorney General of Canada, 1932 A.C. 514, Viscount Dunedin is reported as saying:
The two taxations, dominion and provincial, can stand side by side without interfering with each other, but as soon as you come to the concomitant

privileges of absolute priority they cannot stand side by side and must clash; consequently the dominion must prevail.
If by imposing income taxation on individuals and corporations, or if by imposing succession duties the federal parliament had overridden its jurisdiction it is easy to imagine what would have happened. As I said a moment ago, it was over thirty years ago that the Conservative party then in power initiated the income tax. Does anyone think that if that legislation had been ultra vires of the federal parliament, during that long period from 1917 to 1952 some provincial government, especially a Union Nationale government, would not have tested its validity?
There is no use in stressing the point that there has been no attack upon provincial autonomy. Provincial autonomy has no more been affected thereby at the present time than it was in 1917 when the bill was introduced by the Conservative minister of finance, Sir Thomas White. As I mentioned a few moments ago, there has been a substantial evolution in the political set-up since confederation. There is no doubt that the provinces owe a debt of gratitude to the supreme court and the privy council which bodies did not quite follow the wishes of Sir John A. Macdonald. On the contrary, these courts went as far as they could go to restore the autonomy of the provinces, more especially by invoking the clause in section 92 of the British North America Act respecting property and civil rights. I also believe and am convinced that the head of the government, his ministers and the members of this party do not wish to violate provincial autonomy to any extent.
I am convinced that the present premier of the province of Quebec will agree with me when I say that the cause of provincial autonomy was admirably served and helped by those great Liberal leaders of the province of Quebec, Mercier, Gouin, and Taschereau. These men never failed at any time to be the convinced champions of minority rights and of provincial autonomy well understood and liberally conceived. In speaking tonight in this House of Commons I am proud to repeat that there is no member of the Liberal party who wants to encroach on provincial autonomy.

My colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) spoke at considerable length yesterday concerning the case of Brigadier Connelly, a gentleman who was born in my home community of Calgary. He has made a substantial contribution to this country of ours during his long years of military service. May I say that I endorse completely the statements made by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I say that, having had an opportunity over the past few weeks to study the Connelly case very thoroughly. I have seen much of the correspondence relating to that particular affair. It is a disgrace to Canada that this very able officer, who since his graduation from the Royal Military College has used his engineering and military training in a career of service to this nation, should now be suddenly booted out of the army and his service lost to Canada. This has happened merely because the Ottawa government believes that a political error on its part should be covered up by making Brigadier Connelly the goat. I believe this government should, without further delay, rectify the serious error it has made and clear the name of a very able soldier.
It is not often that a member from Calgary asks for something for his particular community. However, tonight I should like to comment briefly on two things.

The mayor of Calgary has presented to the government a proposal for the joint financing by the city of Calgary and the federal government, of a new terminal for the Calgary airport. Incidentally, this airport is the fifth busiest in Canada. It is the busiest airport between Toronto on the east and Vancouver on the west. When the runways were lengthened three years ago we were required to relinquish the services of a fairsized terminal building. Since that time old shacks which were used during the last war by the United States air force have been used as terminal facilities. For an airport as busy as this one, it is a disgrace that the port of entry to a very progressive community such as Calgary should have as terminal facilities a sizeable but most inadequate tarpaper shack. The Address-Mr. Nickle
The other question concerns something which has been hanging fire for six or seven months. Apparently it takes that length of time to get something accomplished through the rather lengthy mass of red tape separating defence officials in Calgary from those in the national capital at Ottawa. This has to do with the community of Altadore in southwest Calgary, built by the defence department to accommodate the married men and their families from Currie military barracks. Unfortunately, due to an oversight, presumably by the Ottawa authorities, storm sewers were not provided. The result was that, in the midst of this modern community in the city of Calgary, there developed a large slough which has been a source of danger and inconvenience to many of the service families residing near Currie barracks.
Some months ago the city of Calgary offered to split the cost of the installation of storm sewers, which would bring about the removal of that slough and enable that new part of our city to function in the normal way. I am glad to say that, after a great many complaints from the service families in the district and strong requests from the city of Calgary, a few days ago the federal government apparently finally passed an order in council to provide for its contribution of $105,000 toward the cost of constructing these storm sewers. This will now clear the way for the city of Calgary to go ahead, after the completion of the storm sewers, and provide a means of bus transportation by finishing off the road under which that storm sewer will be laid.
Returning to the major issues as I see them, the by-election which brought me to this house last December was decided, I believe, mainly on the issue that this Liberal government was being too liberal with the taxpayers' money, was spending high, wide and handsome, spending wastefully and trying to be Santa Claus by wildly tossing luscious parcels to the Canadian voters, trying to kid the voters into thinking that the money for fancy presents was hoisted from somebody else's piggy bank, not their own.
This brings us to the question of social security, which in essence is the taking by the government of part of the national product to provide greater measures of social security for the underprivileged, the aged, the sick and the maimed. Social security is recognized by the mass of the public and by all political parties as a responsibility of government. On the municipal, provincial and federal level Canada has already gone well along the way to the welfare state. I for one would fight against any retreat from


the social security progress already made, just as would all members in this house.
Like you, I realize also that in the present welfare program there are certain inequalities and injustices to some segments of our population. Some adjustments of a relatively minor nature could and should be made now. However, I firmly believe that Canada cannot now afford any further major steps toward a more complete welfare state. Direct and indirect taxation has for far too long been drawing too heavy a share of the national product. All those who contribute to that national product-the workers in all our businesses and industries and the corporations that are our businesses and industries-are bearing an excessive load of taxation. Our nation is bearing this load partly to provide the essential needs for defence, a spending with which the nation has no quarrel provided waste is eliminated from it. Canada is bearing a federal tax load partly to provide about $1 billion yearly for social security, which is also something that most of us approve. Canada is bearing that load partly to provide a host of essential government services, again without quarrel provided government waste is eliminated from the spending.
The levels of taxation on both personal and corporate incomes help to determine our ability to finance an increasing national productivity and a higher standard of living. Too excessive taxation, regardless of its purpose, is like underfeeding the goose that lays golden eggs. Sometimes it seems to me that it is wiser to defer big-surplus budgeting and more welfare statism and to slash the fat of waste from government spending habits in order to give the goose a full-growth diet and thus boost the golden egg production for years ahead. I believe that time is past due for Canada. You can load a great deal of weight on a pack-horse and get to your destination of greater and more widespread national posterity; but if you overload the pack-horse, meaning the taxpayer, he will sink into the mud of depression, carrying this nation and its hopes with him.
This government, too long in power, has been seeking to extend its tenure by more and fancier handouts, by more and better jobs for party supporters, by lavish passing around of the taxpayers' money and I think also by general extravagance. It is high time that tenure ended, just as the tenure of the free-spending, socialist-minded government has ended in the United States and has also ended in Britain, and Canada had a return to a Conservative and economy-minded government dedicated to letting our citizens keep a larger share of their earnings

to spend and build with as they please, and to leading the nation to the great destiny that can be ours. I believe, of course, that such a government would be one headed by the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, the leader of my party.
There are other alternatives, of course. We have the socialists represented by my friends to my left who are now wooing the citizen taxpayers with the offer of what would be another billion dollars of welfare statism through a costly national health plan and higher old age pensions. There could also be the Social Crediters, the group which was described last night by one of its members as the splinter off the beam.
As to the Social Credit group and their national policy, I must be guided-because I have seen no other statement of national policy recently-by the platform adopted a week or so ago by the Social Crediters meeting in convention in Saskatchewan. At that time they adopted a platform calling for a $100 a month old age pension without a means test, coupled with the raising of tax exemptions to $5,000 for married taxpayers and to $2,500 for single ones. Of course that poses the problem: who is going to pay the shot for the extra $700 or $800 million of pensions? Maybe their answer lies in the nebulous thing called Social Credit dividends, that wondrous currency backed by gosh knows what; but personally I prefer to put more reliance in real dollars.
I notice that on the order paper we have some resolutions from several members of the existing government calling for new and better handouts of various types. All these remind me of a cartoon which I saw recently in the New Yorker magazine and which I should like to see reprinted in Hansard. The cartoon shows a political gathering, with the usual politician spouting lustily from the platform; and in the audience are two ministers of the gospel listening to this politician. One of them turns to the other and says, "Why, that is more than even we can promise them".
Mr. Speaker, I was happy that a day or two ago the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale), when discussing the problems of the west, dealt at some length with the problem of increased population to aid in the building further of western Canada. I want to say that I fully agree with him. I should like to quote briefly from an address on the subject entitled "Building the Future for Western Canada" which I made at Winnipeg a month or so ago. In it I said:
To fully realize the future offered by our natural resources, therefore, we western Canadians must expand our efforts to match our resources with markets . . .
The Address-Mr. Nickle
One phase is to encourage an accelerated rate of immigration to western Canada, not only to provide greater home markets for our products, but also to provide the human resources with which to build a much broader industrial potential. An enlarged program of selective immigration of men and women of pioneering temperament and a wide range of knowledge and special skills is essential to the long-range planning of a still brighter western future.
I trust that this government will greatly enlarge its efforts to ensure that the west and all Canada, in fact, will reach this great objective of 20 million, 25 million or 35 million people before the end of this century.
At the present time we have under way in London a conference of commonwealth prime ministers. Regardless of politics, I am sure the Canadian delegation carries with it the hope of all in this house and all in this country that they will come back with great results which will bring market expansion. However, I noticed in the Ottawa Journal tonight a Canadian Press story dealing with the conference, and in it there is one statement that may be taken with considerable concern in the west. The Canadian Press statement dealing with the commonwealth conference reads in part:
In the case of wheat, for instance, it was noted that in 1950-51 the sterling area imported 5,400,000 tons from dollar sources, principally Canada, at a cost of $490 million. The ministers agreed that increased wheat production is needed particularly in such countries as Pakistan, India and Australia.
It is understood that Canadian officials take no objection to increased commonwealth production of wheat, one of Canada's leading products.
This is what concerns me.
For one thing, Canada is "bullish" about wheat at the moment, and for another Canadian ministers have always said that all they want is a free market run.
I am sure every wheat producer of western. Canada and of the east hopes that the apparent optimism of the government as to its ability to find markets for the growing wheat surplus of the west will be rewarded with success.
In this morning's paper there was another headline, whose background means far more than is implied in the words of the headline itself. It reads: "Plan to extend west pipe line to Sarnia". Back of this announcement made in Toronto today is the start on a third major pipe-line project to serve western Canadian oil. With this particular project, and in the expansion of lines to be tied in with that project across western Canada, will come a transport system for oil adequate, when they reach full capacity, to handle at least 40 per cent more oil than the entire petroleum consumption of this country.
It may be of some interest to this house to know that during the first ten and one-half

year to an average of 162,000 barrels a
The Address-Mr. Nickle months of this year western Canada has been coming through with a rather remarkable record. During those months this year 155 new discoveries of either oil or gas were recorded in the western provinces. It included some 80 oil discoveries, 64 discoveries of natural gas, plus 11 discoveries of wet gas or gas laden with liquid products. This rate of discovery, about one every two days, is 50 per cent higher than the former all-time Canadian record set in 1951. It will interest this house to know, I am sure, that in this string of discoveries the four western provinces have shared. Alberta came through with 118 discoveries of various types. Saskatchewan, as a new oil province, has come through with 25 discoveries this year of oil and gas; northeastern British Columbia, another new oil province, has come through with nine discoveries of oil or gas this year. Southwest Manitoba has come through with three more oil discoveries.
Among the great discoveries of this year, which account for this announcement concerning the new expansion of pipe lines, is the discovery in Fort St. John, northeastern British Columbia, of a natural gas field already proved to contain something over 1,300 billion cubic feet of natural gas. And in central Alberta has come a discovery of the Bonnie Glen-Pigeon Trend field. It contains, on the basis of knowledge to date, a minimum of 250 million barrels of crude oil. This year western Canada is going to record the greatest increase in proved reserves of oil and gas in the history of this country. Oil reserves, for example, for 1952 are going to increase about 500 million barrels, to a total of about 2 billion barrels by the end of this year. Natural gas reserves this year are going to increase about 3,500 billion cubic feet to around 10J thousand billion cubic feet by the year's end. These figures may mean a little more to you when I tell you that back in 1946, only six years ago, our west had oil reserves of only some 65 million barrels, and gas reserves of something like 2,000 billion cubic feet.
More important than the discoveries of oil and gas, with their gross value of more than $5 billion, are the beacons they have lit pointing the way to the future. Our reserves have been developed by an intensity of exploration less than 5 per cent of that in the United States oil states. Undoubtedly ultimate Canadian oil and gas reserves will be several and perhaps many times those proved today.
The oil potential, or our ability to produce out west, has climbed by the present day to something like 280,000 barrels a day. Our actual oil production has climbed this

day. In other words we are running well behind production, compared with actual ability to produce. In the light of this situation and the growing reserves and discoveries that have been made since last spring, there have been two important pipeline developments. One was the start of the construction of an $80 million pipe line across the Rocky mountains from Edmonton to Vancouver. That pipe line, I may say, will be completed next August, and the first oil by pipe line to reach Vancouver refineries will start servicing the market on the coast next October.
A few weeks ago it was announced that on the Pacific coast, in the state of Washington, just south of Vancouver, a $35 million oil refinery would be erected to use Alberta crude oil. The Washington refinery will be completed in the summer of 1954. Word has also come in recent days of the purchase of a refinery site by another major United States oil company in the general Seattle area, and it is reasonably assumed that in the not too distant future plans will be announced for a second United States oil refinery to use our oil on the Pacific coast.
With the growing oil reserve potential, I might say that during this coming year our ability to produce oil will climb to at least
350,000	barrels a day; it will climb in 1954 to probably beyond 400,000 barrels a day, and in 1955 our ability to produce may pass half a million barrels a day, or the equivalent of self-sufficiency for Canada.
With these growing reserves there has been a great deal of concern as to where the oil would go beyond the Pacific coast and the markets west of the existing interprovincial oil pipe line from Alberta through to Superior, Wisconsin, the head of the great lakes area. Today comes the announcement of what is going to be done. A 630-odd mile oil pipe line, 30 inches in diameter, capable of carrying at its peak more than 350,000 barrels of oil a day, will be started immediately from Superior, Wisconsin, across northern Michigan, across the four-mile wide Mackinac strait, through central Michigan and across the St. Clair river at Sarnia, Ontario. That pipe line will be built and placed in operation within one year. So far as our prairie provinces oil producers are concerned, it will open the way for a year-round direct market into Ontario; and so far as Sarnia is concerned, the hon. member for that constituency will perhaps be interested to know that the development of a direct route by pipe line to Sarnia ensures that city's place in the scheme of things,

so that it will likely become the greatest single oil and chemical refining centre in eastern Canada.
This oil pipe line that is being started across United States territory to Sarnia is going to cost something like $75 million. Arrangements to finance that project are now being completed. The necessary steel,
160.000	tons, has recently been allocated by the United States department of defence production. Coupled with this pipe line construction will be a further expansion of the existing interprovincial pipe line leading to the great lakes. Over the next two to four years, depending on the rate of oil reserve growth and the rate of development of oil markets, will come the spending of about $200 million to provide an eastward pipe-line system from Alberta to Ontario and the Detroit region of the United States capable of handling something over
350.000	barrels of oil a day. The Pacific coast pipe line is now being completed and will be in operation next August. It is designed to handle ultimately something over 200,000 barrels of oil per day.
With the several pipe-line systems under construction or well on the way there will be developed an oil transport system capable of handling at the peak more than 650,000 barrels of oil per day. When the west can produce that volume and the markets of this country and our neighbour to the south can consume that amount of oil, Canada will be more than self-sufficient for the first time in her history so far as petroleum is concerned.
As to natural gas, we have had a lot of discussion on this matter during the past session and previously, and I am not going to go into it in any detail. I am happy to say that at the present time a survey, financed by private capital, is being carried out by a great United States university and a university in the province of Ontario. A study will be made of the entire fuel picture of eastern Canada and of the best methods of matching the fuel reserves in western Canada and in the United States with the great market of eastern Canada.
A few days ago the president of Shell Oil Company of Canada, W. M. V. Ash, made an address in Montreal which contains some thoughts on the question of natural gas that I think are worth repeating to this house. Of course he was speaking as the head of one of the large companies which have played a material part in the exploration for and development of oil and gas reserves
The Address-Mr. Nickle in western Canada. Speaking in Montreal on November 20 Mr. Ash said:
As a producer of both oil and gas therefore I would urge with all the force at my command that those responsible for framing Canada's gas policy should base it on fundamental economic principles. After gas reserves have been set aside for the foreseeable local needs, including new industry, let our first and most valuable gas be delivered to the nearest and greatest market, where the best price can be had. Later, as we develop further gas, let us look to the more distant and marginal markets.
Today the picture seems to shape up like this. Substantial reserves have been found in northwestern Alberta and in the northeastern portion of British Columbia, and additions to these reserves are being discovered almost daily. Canadian and provincial permits have been given to one pipe line company which in effect dedicate these reserves of gas to movement to Vancouver and southward to U.S. markets. Percentage-wise, it is anticipated that about 85 per cent of the gas will be delivered to the U.S. markets. The necessary U.S. permits for the on-movement beyond the border are presently the subject of hearings before the U.S. federal power commission. Their award will depend on the answer to the question-do adequate proven reserves exist in the north to satisfy the large northwestern United States demand? Personally I am confident that the strong and growing exploration activity, which is steadily pressing further north, will inevitably prove more than enough reserves of gas. On the other hand delay may cause the insistent demand to be supplied from other sources and that market will be lost forever to Canada.
That is a statement which this government as well as the governments of Alberta and British Columbia might well take to heart. Mr. Ash continues:
Thus while this dedication of the northwestern Alberta and northeast British Columbia reserves to the Vancouver and southward movement seems a logical and sensible move by the authorities, since it is difficult to visualize any other economic market to which those reserves can go, nevertheless this will not provide for the marketing of the large quantities of gas which will be produced with oil throughout the body of Alberta.
To avoid such a situation there has been a school of thought which advocates a trunk line from north to south through Alberta and thence either east or west. Such a system would tap all of Alberta's gas reserves, it would make gas available to a maximum number of Albertans, and in effect would pool Alberta's gas for movement to any market, domestic or otherwise, in any direction.
The questions whether that direction should be east or west, whether any eastern movement should be intra-Canada or should include United States outlets, and other problems, have divided the parties according to two opposing philosophies. The one advocates that western gas, after serving prairie communities, should seek the nearest and largest markets south of the border. The other aims to keep Canadian gas wholly on our side of the border, would serve the same prairie communities, but from Winnipeg would cross relatively sparsely populated terrain over a long and expensive route to Toronto and possibly Montreal. The cost of such gas, unless subsidized, either by the western or the eastern taxpayer, or both, is substantially greater than the cost of gas from American sources.
Possibly the philosophy inherent in the second of these two schemes is not surprising in these

The Address-Mr. Nickle times when nationalism is the cry all over the world. I hope that in our country economic and not isolationist principles will prevail. In the long view surely it is best, not only for Canada's gas producing industry but for Canada at large, to sell its raw material in the most profitable market and to use the revenue obtained thereby to purchase equivalent energy from the most economic sources available to it.
With that quotation from the remarks of Mr. Ash, president of Shell, I shall close my comments on gas. However, I should like to state that in discussing gas going to various markets one prime concern is the price received at the Alberta or prairie end of the pipe line. It has been said that our present reserves are something like ten trillion cubic feet, or ten thousand billion. With that volume of gas a difference of one cent per thousand cubic feet in the price means a difference of $100 million to the Canadian economy. An uneconomic gas pipe line might mean a difference of from two to perhaps five cents per thousand cubic feet. In other words, the difference to the economy of this country might be anywhere from $100 million to $500 million based upon the presently known reserves.
In this connection it might be interesting to have a break-down of where that extra $100 million represented by a difference of one cent in the price of the gas would go. About $15 million would go to the owners of the royalties, mainly the Alberta government. Taking the balance of $85 million and considering our present corporation tax rates and the fact that this would come off the top, more than $42 million would be lost in the way of corporation tax income to the federal government. The balance of around $43 million would represent extra income which the oil or gas producers could use for further expansion, exploration or development; or it would represent dividends to those who are paying the major part of the shot for this tremendous development in western Canada or to the foreign investors and shareholders of so many small and large oil and gas companies.
In his concluding remarks in Montreal Mr. Ash dealt with a subject which I have discussed before in this house. I should like to close with his words in regard to that subject. He said:
When you add to this the fact that the eastern Canadian markets of Toronto and Montreal can be served by American gas at a substantial saving over western Canadian gas, surely every effort should be made by our nation, and by our neighbours to the south, to work out a pooling or "unification", or exchange of the continent's gas supplies.
The same principle has been followed to date and is being followed for the future in


the planning for the matching of oil reserves and markets in Canada and the United States.
