speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Deslieres);, and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. If I were to say more I would only be repeating what has been said already about these two hon. members. It is always of interest to me to hear the speech from the throne read, and I am sure that it pictures for each and every one of us some of the things that we expect will come to pass in the coming year. I was particularly interested to note that one of the subjects about which I had spoken in the house was included in the speech from the throne, namely the question of the rural mail carriers. I am sure some satisfactory arrangement will be made for these men and women who are providing a very creditable service for many people.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the things that are said in this chamber to the ministers of the crown. I have always been amazed at the direct criticism offered to them from which one might assume that the sworn ministers of the crown are not wholly responsible citizens, but I am sure that is not the case. Often opposition members conjure up in the minds of the Canadian people something that is not in true perspective. It is always rather disagreeable for me to have to refer to some of these remarks. However, I note that my good friend, the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White), had the following to say as appears at page 89 of Hansard for November 25:
People do not mind paying for aeroplanes, guns and other supplies for our troops, but I think the people of Canada are getting sick and tired of this arm chair army.
I was obliged to write a note of sympathy to a mother in my community whose son made the supreme sacrifice in Korea. I am sure in her mind and in the minds of her friends that son did not belong to the arm chair army referred to by the hon. member. On page 182 of Hansard for November 28 I find that my very good friend the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) has painted another picture of the things that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) are doing for our armed services. He has painted a picture of 37 miles of carpet which would be quite a waste if only used to take light exercise. I would say that if there was a rug beside

the bed of that soldier who lost his life in Korea the people would not object to it having been placed there.
Last summer I had the privilege of having dinner with one of our servicemen. He told me among other things that he was going up to the icecap of Canada to serve his country. He also told me that when he got to Churchill he would only be half-way to his destination. He left his wife behind him and went there to serve Canada. If the government chooses to provide some of the amenities of life for men who are willing to do such things, we should not complain.
I would also say that there is hardly a man in any of the three armed services today who could not leave that service and enjoy, with the labour force of Canada, the greatest period of earning that anyone could possibly have. The dominion bureau of statistics has this to say:
Canadian labour income reached an all-time monthly peak of $922 million in August-
That is this year.
-as compared with $833 million in the same month last year.
I say, therefore, that these men are leaving their arm chairs behind them and making a great contribution to Canada and the security of the nation. When the members of the opposition point to those on the other side who are responsible for the direction of the defence effort they must do so having it in mind that three fingers are pointing back toward them, because we were told in the house only two days ago that at the beginning of world war II the government was criticized for not doing enough. Now they are criticized for providing too many things. That is the way I view some of the criticism being levelled at our senior cabinet ministers.
The hon. member for Middlesex East also referred to the taxes levied against a farm in his county. He indicated the increase that had taken place. I think it is a good defence of the spending of the government. Each and every one of us pay taxes. I also happen to be engaged in the occupation of farming. My taxes have increased, but that is because I had asked for better drainage and better roads, because we have better accommodation in our schools. I and the other people of my municipality asked for these things. So far as industry is concerned, I was speaking with an industrialist of the city of Chatham right after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had paid his visit to that city. The industrialist said to me, "I appreciate very much the position of the Minister of Finance because different sections of my industry come to me and say that so much
The Address-Mr. Huffman money is needed for expansion and development." He said, "We add all these expenses together and the price tag is put on the article as it leaves my plant." That is the way that we are financing the preparedness effort that is being put forward on behalf of Canada.
Now I would like to refer to my own particular part of the country, the part I represent. I come from a very diversified agricultural area. There are some 19 or 20 specialized crops and they often need special attention. I believe one thing that could assist us a great deal in that area-and we expect a survey to be made on the river Thames- would be to have more ships pass up and down the river, as was the case when this river was open to traffic. We could then get a storage terminal which would assist us to overcome the congestion that comes from time to time when special crops are being harvested. That is one of the things that could be of assistance to our community.
At this time there is one crop that is particularly pertinent and on which I would like to delay the house for a few moments by referring to its history. The sugar industry is of great importance to our economy and provides an annual purchasing power of some $120 million. This was the amount paid for material and services in 1951. The sugar beet industry was established permanently at the turn of the century after some unsuccessful attempts. The sugar refinery located at Chatham is the largest of its kind in Canada and has earned for the city the title, "The sweetest city on earth". The sugar company employs during the refining season some 1,200 people and maintains a permanent staff for its operations. In southern Ontario there are some 6,200 growers. One-half are in the county of Kent. This company provides an annual purchasing power of $11 million for services and the raw products based on 1951 operations. You will note the benefits an industry of this nature brings to any community of Canada.
All the beets for the production of beet sugar are grown locally, providing employment for many people, especially our new Canadians, and this has helped to assimilate many of our immigrants into the fabric of our communities. We have encouraged immigration. The Canada and Dominion Sugar Company of Chatham have had a prime interest in establishing many of our new citizens. They have indicated in their publications their appreciation of the assistance that was given to them by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the Department of Labour. It would be unfortunate to have an industry of this size disrupted to such an extent that


1950 we imported $76 million worth of sugar; in 1951, $75 million; and this year, if the last quarter is on a par with the first three quarters, we will expend around $50 million. This action was duplicated, no doubt, by all importing countries.

speechtext: You are talking about raw sugar.

speechtext:
I refer to raw sugar. The international bank for reconstruction and development has stated:
Cuba has expanded sugar production at the expense of soil fertility and water supply. They also contend they are in a precarious position through failure to diversify agricultural production.
I contend we are encouraging this condition by taking sugar from their surplus production. I also contend we are limiting diversification of our agricultural production, as this purchased surplus will result in lower sugar beet acreage across Canada. The sugar industry is located from the Pacific to the Atlantic. It is designed to refine the sugar requirements of Canada, and has done this in the past, as we have imported very limited amounts of refined sugar. It is the employer of Canadian labour. It is Canadian knowhow, Canadian investment to a large extent. The sugar beet part of the industry is 100 per cent Canadian. We will never in the future of Canada produce enough sugar beets to meet the domestic requirements. This is not true of many agricultural crops. The government of Canada has lent assistance to market surplus crops in the past. This condition can be alleviated by encouraging more non-surplus crops. The production of sugar beets is at the moment carried on in four provinces, Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec and Ontario.
Many were of the opinion that the contract for Cuban raw sugar was designed so that it would earn dollars and assist Cuba to purchase greater quantities of our basic production.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. We find their purchases of oats down 50 per cent from 1951; flour down 50 per cent for the same period; malt up 27 per cent; seed potatoes up 40 per cent, but the total is small; codfish, no change; machinery up 40 per cent; copper up 4J times or 10 per

cent of total exports. There are other items which have altered very little. This indicates the balance of trade was derived from materials, not basic production.
Our people have no complaint regarding the importing of raw sugar from Cuba, and if it is thought that the amount of refined sugar, namely the 30 million pounds exported to us this year, is the correct amount for Cuba to supply, let this be added to the Cuban contract. This would make the amount
90,000	tons instead of 75,000. But I must say I am partial to empire sources of supply.
The United States government of late imports almost all the sugar requirements of that country on a quota basis, first knowing their consumption, and then analysing their sugar beet production. Then quotas for raw sugar imports are set. This procedure does away with the fluctuation caused by unusual amounts of sugar being brought in unnecessarily. Imports of refined sugar have caused a stockpiling by our local company. If it had not been for the progressive views held by the sugar company, and the building of cylindrical silos to store the bulk sugar, they would not have been in a position to accommodate this year's production.
It is very evident Cuba is employing a determined effort to dispose of this year's crop. I note that H. R. Mackeson, British secretary for overseas trade, stated:
The government in the United Kingdom is determined not to buy more Cuban sugar than they are at present."
In March of this year representatives of the governments of producing areas and the sugar industry met in London. On September 29 the inter-sugar conference opened in London, and on this occasion it is understood Cuba was seeking control of prices-no doubt through some influence of the international bank for reconstruction and development. If Cuba wishes now to avoid chaos in the sugar industry, it is important to us that her earlier actions do not further disrupt our domestic sugar industry. Our growers have a participating sugar beet contract. The price they receive is related to the sale of sugar and plant by-products. This session I recall the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) suggesting that if industry wish to have good
The Address-Mr. Huffman relations with labour, they should share their returns. May I say this form of contract has been in effect for some time in this industry.
I have stated some of the reasons for the position the industry finds itself in today. May I state some of the things that could be done to overcome the problem. It has been suggested by grower associations that a quota system for imports of raw sugar would prevent the unfortunate condition in which the industry now finds itself. Some might feel the consumer would be the forgotten person, but I believe there are two safeguards. First, the refiners of Canada would have to buy in competition. Second, if there were no competition at the wholesale level the office of the combines investigation commission could see that there was no special arrangement between companies.
The producer of sugar beets would then be safeguarded against the position in which he finds himself. This year, after producing the crop with labour costs estimated on returns for 1951, he now finds the return per acre considerably reduced due to importations of Cuba's surplus crop and the decline in his participating contract.
Adopting the quota system would provide for the raw sugar exporters a calculated amount of import requirements. It would do away with unnecessary importations of sugar, and stabilize the entire industry. Canada is moving toward stabilization in many phases of her economy. We listened to the announcement that will help stabilize the gold industry. The international wheat agreement has a stabilizing effect on wheat. Subsidies for farm products have had the same effect. These references could be enlarged.
I trust that this is a reasoned and reasonable resume of an important industry, and with co-operation we can attain a satisfactory solution.
